Geotechnical Staff Engineer

GeotechStaffEngineer

User Manual for the practicing geotechnical engineer
A toolkit that turns the staff engineer’s repertoire into composable, machine-callable methods, wraps them in a probabilistic variability engine, and drives them with an engine-agnostic reasoning agent — because in geotechnical engineering the true answer is a distribution, not a single number.
Version 5.33.0
36 analysis modules · 34 digitized references · 1535 agent-callable methods
FOSM / PEM / Monte Carlo / FORM reliability · validated against published benchmarks

Professional-use disclaimer

Read this first

GeotechStaffEngineer is an analysis and research aid — a multiplier for a qualified engineer’s judgment, not a replacement for it, and not a design deliverable.

Geotechnical engineering is the practice of building on and in the ground, where the material is the earth itself: heterogeneous, layered, partly saturated, and sampled at only a handful of points across a site. Because the ground is variable and only partly known, a single number is never the answer. This toolkit exists to help an engineer run the industry-standard methods repeatedly across plausible subsurface and loading conditions and understand the range and spread of answers. It does not know your site, and it cannot exercise engineering judgment.

What this software is — and is not

  • It is a library of deterministic methods, a probabilistic variability engine, digitized references, and an LLM agent that drives them.
  • It is not a stamped design, a professional opinion, or a substitute for site-specific investigation, characterization, and review.
  • Using this software creates no engineer-of-record relationship and no professional engagement with the authors or contributors.

Your responsibilities as a user

  • A qualified, licensed professional engineer familiar with the site must independently review every input, assumption, method selection, and result before it is relied upon. Outputs are candidate calculations to be checked, not conclusions to be adopted.
  • Confirm that the method applies to your problem. Every method has applicability limits, sign conventions, and edge cases — documented in each module’s DESIGN.md (and, where present, VALIDATION.md).
  • Confirm the inputs and units. All quantities are SI (meters, kPa, kN, kN/m, degrees). Mixed or mis-scaled units are the user’s responsibility to catch.
  • Treat LLM-agent output with particular care. The agent can select the wrong method, mis-transcribe a value, or read a chart imperfectly. Its answers are a starting point for review, never a final basis for design.

Validation scope

Selected modules are validated against published worked examples and benchmarks (Fredlund & Krahn 1977, ACADS, Duncan, Griffiths & Lane, the Prandtl solution, and GEC / Caltrans / FLAC examples). The specific problems checked and their verdicts are recorded in validation_examples/RESULTS.md and the per-module VALIDATION.md files. Validation covers only those documented cases. Agreement on a benchmark does not certify correctness for any other geometry, parameter range, or loading condition.

No warranty

This software is provided under the MIT License “AS IS”, WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND, express or implied. In no event shall the authors or copyright holders be liable for any claim, damages, or other liability arising from its use. Responsibility for the safety, adequacy, and code-compliance of any design remains entirely with the licensed professional engineer who adopts it.

Chapter 1What this package is

Geotechnical engineering is the practice of building on and in the ground — foundations, retaining walls, slopes, excavations, embankments. Unlike a steel beam with a certified strength, the geotechnical engineer’s material is the earth itself: heterogeneous, layered, partly saturated, and sampled at only a handful of points across an entire site. Because the ground is variable and only partly known, a single number is never the answer.

Understanding a geotechnical problem means understanding how the answer moves as the inputs move. Analysis is repeated calculation across plausible subsurface and loading conditions — running a chained assortment of industry-standard formulas, empirical correlations, and numerical methods, comparing against the design requirements, and varying assumptions until the design is robust across the uncertainty. The engineer’s job is to understand the range and spread of answers, not one point estimate. The true answer is a distribution.

1.1 What a geotechnical engineer actually does

StepActivityReality
CharacterizeDrill borings, push CPT cones, run lab testsA sparse, noisy picture of strength, stiffness, and groundwater — never the whole truth
IdealizeCollapse the data into a layered soil profileDesign values of φ, c, γ, water table — each an estimate with a spread
AnalyzeRun the method (bearing, settlement, pile, slope)A chained assortment of standard formulas and numerical methods
Check & reviseCompare to requirements; vary assumptions; re-runLoop until the design is robust across the uncertainty

Steps 3 and 4 are repeated calculations across plausible conditions. This toolkit packages those methods as clean, machine-callable Python and puts a reasoning agent on top so the engineer can explore more of the problem in the time they have.

1.2 The lineage: every tool amplified the engineer

Slide rules and design charts → spreadsheets and FEM → scripting and Monte Carlo → LLM agents. Every tool in this lineage did the same thing: it let one engineer explore more of the problem. This project is the next step — not a replacement for judgment, but a multiplier for it. Take the methods a staff engineer uses, make every one a clean function that returns structured data, wrap the variability tooling around them, and drive them with an agent that reads the standards back to you.

1.3 The architecture in four layers

One stack, layered so each concern stays independent:

LayerWhat it isWhy it’s separate
Agent harnessAn engine-agnostic LLM driver (funhouse_agent) that discovers modules, calls methods, reads figures, and cites referencesThe reasoning that combines methods lives here, not inside the methods
Variability enginereliability — FOSM, PEM, Monte Carlo, FORM → β and Pf, plus a published COV database and spatial averagingOrthogonal: it wraps any deterministic method as a callable and characterizes how its output scatters
Deterministic analysisThe analysis modules — dataclass in, dataclass out, one method per engineering problemIndependent, testable leaves; no analysis module imports another
Shared spine + referencesgeotech_common’s SoilProfile that every module speaks, and the digitized reference libraryOne way to describe the ground; one place to cite the standards
The design rule that makes outputs citable

Everything is SI (m, kPa, kN, kN/m, degrees). Every analyze_*() returns a dataclass with .summary() for human/agent reading and .to_dict() for JSON. Analysis modules never import each other — the routing that combines them lives in the agent layer. That discipline is what lets a result be traced, reviewed, and cited.

Chapter 2Installation & environments

2.1 Install from PyPI

# the whole stack: analysis modules, reference library, deep agent, webapp
pip install geotech-staff-engineer

# everything (all optional analysis backends + the deep agent)
pip install "geotech-staff-engineer[deep,full]"

pip install geotech-staff-engineer

The core install already covers the native modules — bearing capacity, settlement, piles, walls, slope stability, the reliability engine, fem2d, and the reference library (geotech-references is a hard dependency, so DM7/GEC/UFC lookups work out of the box). The optional extras pull in the third-party libraries that the wrapper modules drive. Install only what you need, or take [full].

Honest failure when an extra is missing

Without [full], the roughly one-in-six methods that need an optional backend fail cleanly with a “not installed” message rather than a confusing traceback. Install the matching extra to enable them.

2.3 Local Python

Requires Python 3.10+. The package is pure Python; the only heavy dependencies are numpy and scipy. For the LLM agent you need an engine (see the next chapter) and, for a Claude engine, an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment. Keys are read from the environment at run time — never pass them through a notebook cell or a chat transcript.

2.4 Databricks / Funhouse

Install from a cluster-accessible location — /tmp or a Unity Catalog Volume, not /Workspace (the workspace FUSE mount mangles wheel filenames and does not durably store output files):

%pip install "geotech-staff-engineer"
# or a test wheel uploaded to /tmp or a UC Volume:
%pip install "/tmp/geotech_staff_engineer--py3-none-any.whl"
No compiled meshing dependency

The cross-section and RC-section engines used to wrap sectionproperties and concreteproperties, which both require cytriangle — a compiled wheel corporate package proxies quarantine. A Nexus malware-defense 403 on it failed the entire 5.12.0 install on the cluster, so in 5.13.0 both were re-implemented natively on numpy/scipy: exact closed-form integration for the geometry, published closed forms for torsion, and ACI strain compatibility for the RC section. The retired libraries’ outputs were pinned as regression oracles first; every RC scalar agrees to better than 0.04%.

The typing_extensions / restart-Python note (now handled automatically)

Databricks cluster runtimes pre-import an old typing_extensions (<4.13) at kernel startup, which used to break the langgraph imports behind the [deep] agent with TypeError: TypedDict() got an unexpected keyword argument 'extra_items', requiring dbutils.library.restartPython(). As of v5.4 the package repairs this in place: funhouse_agent.runtime_check.ensure_typing_extensions() runs automatically at the top of the first funhouse_agent.deep import, reloading the freshly-installed typing_extensions≥4.13 so the restart is normally no longer needed. If an even older copy is pinned at cluster scope and the in-place reload can’t win, it raises a clear message that falls back to the restart instruction.

Save calc packages, DXF, and plots to /tmp or a UC Volume and copy them out with dbutils.fs.cp; writes to /Workspace can silently leave an 11-byte placeholder. As of recent releases the file tools defend themselves — they verify the written bytes and return a rescue_path in /tmp if the target did not store the content.

2.5 Reference figures: GEOTECH_REFERENCES_DOCS

The reference figure catalogs (captions, page numbers, cross-links) ship inside the wheel, so figure_search works from a clean install. The source PDF pages are not shipped (large + license). To enable the vision read-off — where the agent renders a catalogued chart and reads a value off it — place the reference PDFs in a folder and set GEOTECH_REFERENCES_DOCS to point at it. On Databricks, copy a docs/ folder of PDFs in and set the variable.

Chapter 3Using the agent

The same validated methods are reachable at three altitudes: import a module and get a dataclass back; wrap that method to return the distribution; or describe the problem in natural language and let the agent run the methods and cite the standards. This chapter is about the third altitude — the agent.

3.1 The v1 agent: GeotechAgent

GeotechAgent is engine-agnostic: it drives any backend that satisfies the small GenAIEngine protocol (a chat() method, optionally analyze_image() for vision). Ship it a Claude engine, a Funhouse PrompterAPI, or a native OpenAI-tool-calling engine.

from funhouse_agent import GeotechAgent, ClaudeEngine, NativeToolEngine

# Claude (reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment)
agent = GeotechAgent(genai_engine=ClaudeEngine())

# Databricks / Funhouse with native OpenAI tool calling (recommended there)
agent = GeotechAgent(genai_engine=NativeToolEngine(fh_prompter))

result = agent.ask("2 m strip footing, 1.5 m deep, sand phi=30, c=10, water at 5 m. "
                   "Bearing capacity and FOS - and how sensitive is it to phi? Cite the method.")
print(result.answer)        # the cited answer
print(result.tool_calls)    # every method the agent ran
print(result.rounds)        # ReAct iterations

3.2 How tool dispatch works

The agent never has to know a method signature in advance. It discovers the toolbox with four dispatch tools, then calls the one it needs:

ToolWhat it returns
list_agents()Every available module with a one-line brief
list_methods(agent, category)The methods on a module, grouped by category
describe_method(agent, method)Full parameter documentation — names, types, required flags, allowed values
call_agent(agent, method, params)Execute the calculation; returns the result dict or a helpful error

The dispatch layer is forgiving by design: a method name the model guesses is resolved through a curated alias map; a value that belongs to a selector parameter (say 'vesic') is redirected to the right call with a directive error; and a genuinely unknown name gets a “did you mean” suggestion. This cut the method-name guessing that otherwise dogs tool-using agents.

3.3 References through a scoped consultant

The primary agent does not call the 21 reference modules directly. Reference access is routed through a single consult_references tool backed by a reference-scoped sub-agent — a second GeotechAgent restricted to the reference modules. This keeps the primary agent’s tool surface small (which measurably cut module-name guessing) while still giving it the full reference library, figure search, and vision read-off on demand. The behavior is set by reference_mode: 'anytime' (default) offers the consultant always; 'after_calc' only after a calculation has run; 'off' keeps the legacy direct-call behavior.

3.4 Vision: reading drawings and charts

When the engine supports images, the agent gains vision tools: analyze_image and analyze_pdf_page for site plans and report pages, and read_reference_figure, which finds a design chart by meaning (figure_search) and then renders the actual page and reads a value off it — rather than answering a chart value from memory. Attach files before asking:

with open("cross_section.pdf", "rb") as f:
    agent.add_attachment("section", f.read())
result = agent.ask("Extract the slope geometry from 'section' and find the FOS by Bishop.")

# direct geometry extraction (bypasses the ReAct loop)
geo = agent.extract_geometry_from_pdf(pdf_bytes, page=0)
geo.surface_points, geo.boundary_profiles

3.5 The v2 deep agent and notebook chat

Installing the [deep] extra unlocks funhouse_agent.deep.build_deep_agent, a deepagents/LangGraph-based loop with the same toolbox and an optional staged, human-gated model-setup sub-agent (off by default). For interactive use in Jupyter or Databricks, NotebookChat (v1) and DeepNotebookChat (v2) give an ipywidgets chat with file upload, collapsible tool calls, and inline calc-package preview:

from funhouse_agent.notebook import NotebookChat
chat = NotebookChat(agent)
chat.display()
chat.attach("/Volumes/proj/site_plan.png")   # or the upload widget
Treat agent output as a first draft

The agent can select the wrong method, mis-transcribe a value, or read a chart imperfectly. Run it with verbose=True or an on_tool_call callback so you can see every method and parameter it used, and review the tool calls — not just the prose — before relying on anything.

4.1 Shallow foundations

Sizing and checking spread footings and mats: how much load the ground carries, and how far it settles.

4.1.1 bearing_capacity — Bearing capacity

Problems it solves

Sizing a spread footing or mat and confirming the ground can carry it: the ultimate bearing capacity, the allowable pressure at a chosen factor of safety, and the sensitivity of both to width, embedment, groundwater, eccentricity, and a layered profile.

Methods & theories implemented
  • General bearing-capacity equation with Nc, Nq, Nγ by Vesic, Meyerhof, or Hansen (selectable); Vesic is the default and the AASHTO/GEC-6 factor set.
  • Terzaghi bearing capacity (general or local shear) with the UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-5 shape factors and no depth or inclination factors (inclined loads and slopes are refused); Nγ after Kumbhojkar (1993) as tabulated in Das by default, or Coduto et al. (2016), the basis of UFC Table 5-2, each named in the result.
  • Shape, depth, load-inclination, base-tilt, and ground-slope correction factors (Vesic form).
  • Eccentric loading via the Meyerhof effective-area (B′, L′) reduction.
  • Two-layer (strong-over-weak / weak-over-strong) bearing with load spread.
  • Groundwater in the failure wedge through an effective-unit-weight model.
  • References: Vesic (1973); Meyerhof (1963); Hansen (1970); FHWA GEC-6 (FHWA-SA-02-054); AASHTO LRFD.
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Bearing Capacity
MethodWhat it doesParams
bearing_capacity_analysisFull bearing capacity analysis for a shallow foundation (Vesic/Meyerhof/Hansen, or Terzaghi 1943 via factor_method='terzaghi').25
bearing_capacity_factorsQuick lookup of Nc, Nq, Ngamma for a given friction angle (Vesic/Meyerhof/Hansen N-gamma, or Terzaghi's factors).4

layer2_friction_anglefloatoptionalSecond layer phi (degrees).
layer2_unit_weightfloatoptionalSecond layer gamma (kN/m3). Triggers 2-layer analysis.

layer2_descriptionstroptionalSecond layer label for the result.

factor_methodstroptionalShape/depth/inclination-factor method. Each takes its own N-gamma unless ngamma_method names another; 'meyerhof' = UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-6, with the shape factors 1 under an inclined load (its note A); it has no base-tilt or ground-slope factors (UFC p. 294, Table 5-3), so base_tilt and ground_slope are refused with it. Hansen applies to N-gamma only: use ngamma_method='hansen'. 'terzaghi' = Terzaghi (1943): his Nc, Nq, N-gamma and shape coefficients (1.3cNc; 0.4/0.3 gamma B Ngamma square/circular), no depth or inclination factors; not for inclined loads, slopes or tilted bases (UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-3). allowed: vesic, meyerhof, terzaghi
ngamma_methodstroptionalNgamma factor method. Default depends on factor_method: the method's own, 'vesic' = 2(Nq+1)tan(phi) (GEC-6 Eq. 5-8), 'meyerhof' = (Nq-1)tan(1.4 phi) (UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-6), 'kumbhojkar' with factor_method='terzaghi'. 'hansen' = 1.5(Nq-1)tan(phi). Another than the method's own is a mixed method; the result's choices say so. With factor_method='terzaghi' (Terzaghi gave N-gamma only as a chart): 'kumbhojkar' (Kumbhojkar 1993 as tabulated in Das) or 'coduto' (Coduto et al. 2016 approximation, UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-2); the result reports the other beside it. allowed: vesic, meyerhof, hansen, kumbhojkar, coduto
failure_modestroptionalfactor_method='terzaghi' only: 'local' applies Terzaghi's local-shear reduction c* = 2/3 c, tan(phi*) = 2/3 tan(phi) (UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-4). allowed: general, local
base_tiltfloatoptionalBase tilt angle (degrees). With factor_method 'vesic' only (GEC-6 Table 5-5 factors); 'meyerhof' and 'terzaghi' have none and refuse it (UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-3).
eccentricity_BfloatoptionalLoad eccentricity along B (m).
eccentricity_LfloatoptionalLoad eccentricity along L (m).
load_inclinationfloatoptionalLoad inclination from vertical (degrees), 0 to below 90; with factor_method 'meyerhof' below phi, as UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-6 takes theta = atan(H/V) < phi' (refused at phi or more).
ground_slopefloatoptionalGround slope angle down from horizontal (degrees), 0 to 45, this tool's own limit: Vesic's g_q = (1 - tan omega)^2 is 0 at 45 deg. With factor_method 'vesic' only; 'meyerhof' and 'terzaghi' have no ground-slope factors and refuse it (UFC 3-220-20 p. 294, Table 5-3). For a footing on or near a slope GEC-6 Sec. 5.2.3.4 uses N_cq and N_gamma-q (Fig. 5-7).
vertical_loadfloatoptionalRequired with factor_method 'vesic', a load_inclination and a soil with cohesion (or phi = 0): the vertical load V on the footing (kN; kN/m for a strip). Vesic's load inclination factors take H = V tan(load_inclination) over V + A' c cot(phi) (Vesic 1975, EN 1997-1:2004 Annex D.4); with c = 0 that is tan(load_inclination) and V cancels. Without it the call is refused (factor_method 'meyerhof' takes the angle alone, UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-6).
depth_factor_methodstroptionalDepth factors for an embedded footing. 'hansen': Brinch Hansen's (1970) k = Df/B below Df/B = 1, arctan(Df/B) from 1 (UFC 3-220-20 Tables 5-7, 5-8 note B) in the factor_method's d factors (Meyerhof's: k = Df/B up to 1 as UFC Table 5-6 prints it); at phi = 0 Vesic's cohesion term adds Table 5-7's d_c = 0.4 k, as UFC Eq. 5-21 does. 'gec6' (factor_method 'vesic' only): GEC-6 Eq. 5-14 and Table 5-4, d_q on the surcharge term alone, 1.0 below Df/B = 1. 'none': no depth factors, as GEC-6 Sec. 5.2.3.3 advises unless the cover over the footing is competent and sure to stay. The result's choices give what each option gives. allowed: hansen, gec6, none
Worked example

Ask → A 2 m × 10 m strip footing bears 1.5 m deep in a c–φ soil (φ=30°, c=10 kPa, γ=18 kN/m³), water 5 m down. What is the bearing capacity and the allowable pressure at FOS = 3?

call_agent(
    agent_name='bearing_capacity',
    method='bearing_capacity_analysis',
    parameters={
        "width": 2.0,
        "length": 10.0,
        "depth": 1.5,
        "shape": "rectangular",
        "cohesion": 10.0,
        "friction_angle": 30.0,
        "unit_weight": 18.0,
        "gwt_depth": 5.0,
        "factor_of_safety": 3.0
    },
)

The result carries every N-, shape-, depth- and inclination factor separately, so a reviewer can trace the number back to the governing terms.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • The high-level compute() applies Vesic depth factors and averages the effective unit weight over the wedge; this runs higher than an example that sets the depth factor to 1.0 (cohesive overburden) or uses an AASHTO Cw groundwater correction — both are defensible conventions (validation V-021).
  • General shear failure is assumed; punching/local shear in very loose or soft soils is not modelled separately.

4.1.2 settlement — Settlement

Problems it solves

How far a foundation settles and how fast: immediate (elastic) movement, primary consolidation of clays, granular settlement of sands, and the settlement–time curve.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Elastic (immediate) settlement with shape/rigidity influence factors.
  • Schmertmann (1978) strain-influence-factor method for granular soils.
  • One-dimensional Cc/Cr e–log p consolidation with layer summation and preconsolidation (NC/OC).
  • Hough (1959) granular C′-index settlement (bearing-capacity index from corrected SPT N′; GEC-6 Fig 5-19).
  • Stress increase by the 2:1 method, Boussinesq, or Westergaard; secondary compression (Cα); Terzaghi time-rate for the settlement–time curve.
  • References: Schmertmann et al. (1978); Hough (1959); Terzaghi 1-D consolidation; FHWA GEC-6.

Worked example

Ask → A 4 m normally-consolidated clay layer (Cc=0.25, e0=0.8) sees a 50 kPa stress increase. How much primary consolidation settlement?

call_agent(
    agent_name='settlement',
    method='consolidation_settlement',
    parameters={
        "layers": [
                {
                        "thickness": 4.0,
                        "depth_to_center": 2.0,
                        "e0": 0.8,
                        "Cc": 0.25,

Layer summation with per-layer stress on the e–log p curve; the same call also accepts a footing width so it computes the 2:1 / Boussinesq stress increase itself.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • The Hough C′ index is the Hough bearing-capacity index, not Cc/(1+e0) — use the consolidation path for cohesive soils and Hough/Schmertmann for granular.

4.2 Deep foundations

Driven piles, drilled shafts, and pile groups — axial capacity, lateral response, drivability, group action, and downdrag.

4.2.1 axial_pile — Axial pile capacity

Problems it solves

Axial capacity of a driven pile in compression (and uplift): the skin friction and toe resistance developed as the pile passes through a layered profile, and how capacity grows with embedment depth.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Nordlund (1963/1979) method for shaft and toe in cohesionless soils (K–δ and correction-factor charts, bearing-capacity-factor toe with the Meyerhof qL limit).
  • Tomlinson / α-method total-stress skin friction in cohesive soils; 9·cu end bearing.
  • β-method effective-stress skin friction for all layers.
  • Groundwater-split effective-stress integration; optional per-layer separate shaft/toe friction angle; below-grade pile head (head_depth); uplift capacity.
  • Pile sections: closed/open pipe, square/circular concrete, and H-piles (with the box perimeter/toe-area convention).
  • References: FHWA GEC-12 (FHWA-NHI-16-064); Nordlund; Tomlinson; validated against the GEC-12 Nordlund/α worked examples (validation V-001/V-002).
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Axial Pile
MethodWhat it doesParams
axial_pile_capacityFull driven pile axial capacity analysis (Nordlund/Tomlinson/Beta).35
capacity_vs_depthCapacity vs depth curve for pile length optimization.34
make_pile_sectionCreate a pile section and return its geometric properties.12

ParameterTypeDescription

gwt_depthfloatoptionalGroundwater depth below ground surface (m).
head_depthfloatoptionalDepth of the pile head below the ground surface (m), e.g. the bottom of a footing 1.5 m down. Layers above the head contribute no skin friction; overburden above the head still raises effective stress at the tip. Default 0 = head at the ground surface.
factor_of_safetyfloatoptionalFactor of safety for the allowable capacity. Default 2.5: FHWA NHI-06-089 Table 9-5 (indicator piles with wave equation analysis); 2.00 with a static load test, 2.25 with dynamic testing, 2.75 wave equation only, 3.50 Gates formula. GEC-12 itself designs by resistance factors: the result also gives the factored resistance (Table 7-1, Eq. 7-3).
methodstroptionalauto = by soil type: the Nordlund method in cohesionless soil (GEC-12 Sec. 7.2.1.3.1), the alpha method with Tomlinson's adhesion in cohesive soil (Sec. 7.2.1.3.2); beta = the beta (effective stress) method in every layer (Sec. 7.2.1.3.4). allowed: auto, beta
include_upliftbooloptionalAlso report uplift (tension) capacity.
cohesive_phifloatoptionalFALLBACK drained phi' (deg) for cohesive layers under method='beta' (skin AND tip); a per-layer friction_angle on a cohesive layer wins over this global.
uplift_skin_fractionfloatoptionalFraction of the outside side resistance taken in uplift (with include_uplift). Default 1.0: GEC-12 Eq. 7-38 takes the whole shaft resistance and puts the uplift reduction in the resistance factor; 0.7 is the customary share in free-draining soils GEC-12 cites.
pile_weightfloatoptionalPile self-weight (kN) added to uplift capacity (with include_uplift).
toe_stress_limitfloatoptionalLimit on sigma'p at the toe for the Nordlund toe resistance (kPa). Default 143.6 kPa = 3 ksf, GEC-12 Step 8; null for no limit (GEC-12's worked example did not limit it).
inside_friction_ratiofloatoptionalOpen-end pipe, unplugged case: interior over exterior unit side resistance. Default 1/3, the low end of GEC-12's 'typically on the order of 1/3 to 1/2' (Sec. 7.10.7).
open_pipe_toe_limitfloatoptionalOpen-end pipe in cohesionless soil: limiting unit toe resistance (kPa). Default 5027 kPa = 105 ksf (Tomlinson, GEC-12 Sec. 7.10.7); null for none.
open_pipe_methodstroptionalOpen-end pipe: 'auto' takes Tomlinson's Eq. 7-90 for a pipe under 24 in with the toe in clay and over half its length in clay (GEC-12 p. 407), else the lesser of the plugged and unplugged cases (Eqs. 7-88/7-89, 'paikowsky_whitman'). allowed: auto, paikowsky_whitman, tomlinson
cohesive_Ntfloatoptionalmethod='beta': Nt of a cohesive toe layer. Default 3 (GEC-12: a relatively low Nt in clays unless local correlations suggest higher; Table 7-9 clay 3-30). A layer's own Nt wins.
h_pile_toe_areastroptionalH-pile toe area: 'box' (depth x flange width, GEC-12 Sec. 7.10.7) or 'steel'. GEC-12 Step 9 leaves it to past experience and local load tests. allowed: box, steel
adhesion_curvestroptionalalpha-method: GEC-12 Fig. 7-17 curves. 'auto' = smooth steel for pipe piles, the concrete/timber/corrugated curve for H-piles (GEC-12 p. 247) and concrete or timber piles. allowed: auto, concrete_timber_corrugated, smooth_steel
adhesion_beyond_chartstroptionalalpha method where a clay layer's su is past the end of the chart's curves (Fig. 7-17, or 7-18 where read); GEC-12 p. 247 and alpha-method Step 1 recommend API RP 2A's alpha there for highly overconsolidated clays. 'api_if_highly_overconsolidated': API alpha in a layer whose su / sigma'vo is at or above highly_overconsolidated_su_ratio, Ca held at the curve's end below it; 'chart_end': Ca held at the curve's end in every such layer (GEC-12's worked example, Vol 3 Table D-100); 'api': API alpha in every such layer. Within the curves Ca is read off Fig. 7-17 as drawn (it can exceed su). allowed: api_if_highly_overconsolidated, chart_end, api
highly_overconsolidated_su_ratiofloatoptionalalpha method: the su / sigma'vo at and above which a clay is highly overconsolidated, for adhesion_beyond_chart 'api_if_highly_overconsolidated'. GEC-12 gives no value; it is the engineer's judgment, so a run with a clay layer whose su is past the chart's curves is refused until this (or adhesion_beyond_chart 'chart_end' or 'api') is given. Ask the user, or state the value taken as a judgment call.
displaced_volumefloatoptionalNordlund displaced volume V per unit length (m3/m). Default: the steel area of an H-pile, the gross area of other piles (an open pipe as a closed pipe; its steel area, if it drives unplugged, is below GEC-12 Fig. 7-9).
pile_areafloatoptionalCustom section (m2): the cross-section area, the steel of an H-pile or a closed pipe, the gross area of a concrete or timber pile (it gives the Nordlund displaced volume of an H-pile and of a solid pile). With pile_perimeter and pile_width it replaces diameter, wall_thickness, width or designation; pile_type still picks the GEC-12 curves (not for pipe_open: its section comes from diameter and wall_thickness).
pile_perimeterfloatoptionalCustom section: the perimeter for the side resistance (m); the box perimeter of an H-pile (GEC-12 Steps 6 and p. 247).
pile_tip_areafloatoptionalCustom section: the toe area (m2). Required for h_pile (its box area; h_pile_toe_area 'steel' takes pile_area) and pipe_closed (the gross area); a concrete or timber pile's is its pile_area when not given.
pile_widthfloatoptionalCustom section: the width or diameter b (m), an H-pile's flange width; for D/b and the width notes.
pile_depthfloatoptionalCustom section: the section's depth (m), an H-pile's; reported only.
pile_namestroptionalCustom section: its name, e.g. 'HP16x101'.
adhesion_chartstroptionalalpha-method chart (GEC-12 p. 246): 'fig_7_17' (Tomlinson's Ca, recommended generally), 'fig_7_18' (Tomlinson's alpha for each clay layer's stratigraphy case: sand or sandy gravel over stiff clay, soft clay over stiff clay, stiff clay alone) or 'smaller' (the smaller Ca of the two in each layer, which p. 246 advises the inexperienced user to take). A layer's case is its fig_7_18_case, else from the profile: cohesive layers under a cohesionless layer the sand case, from the ground surface the stiff-clay case; the soft-clay case only where a layer gives it. Eq. 7-90 (open pipe) takes Ca from Fig. 7-17 whatever this is (p. 407). allowed: fig_7_17, fig_7_18, smaller
shrink_swell_depthfloatoptionalDepth (m below the ground surface) of a shrink-swell zone: no shaft resistance in cohesive soil above it (GEC-12 p. 247). Default none.
beta_coefficientsstroptionalmethod='beta': beta and Nt where a layer gives none: GEC-12 Table 7-9 by the layer's soil_class (clay 0.15-0.35, silt 0.25-0.50, sand 0.30-0.90, gravel 0.35-0.80; Steps 2b/5b), a straight line in phi' between Table 7-9's range ends (the module's reading; the table prints only the ends). A clay toe takes cohesive_Nt. GEC-12 prints no beta formula from phi' alone; give a layer's beta and Nt for other values (local experience, Steps 2a/5a). allowed: table_7_9
toe_phi_zonestroptionalNordlund toe: the phi near the toe. 'toe_layer' (the toe layer's toe_friction_angle or friction_angle) or 'average_3b' (averaged over the cohesionless soil from the toe to 3b below, GEC-12 Step 7c's zone). allowed: toe_layer, average_3b

                },
                {
                        "thickness": 12.0,
                        "soil_type": "cohesionless",
                        "unit_weight": 19.0,
                        "friction_angle": 36.0
                }
        ],
        "gwt_depth": 5.0,
        "factor_of_safety": 2.5
    },
)

Applicability limits & conventions
  • The Tomlinson α–cu curve runs conservative in the stiff-clay band (α≈0.42 vs DrivenPiles ≈0.76 at su≈1.9 ksf) — a defensible curve choice, documented, not tuned (V-002).
  • Datum matters: reference the profile to the pile head (e.g. a below-grade footing) so no spurious skin friction is added above the head.

4.2.2 lateral_pile — Lateral pile analysis

Problems it solves

Lateral response of a pile or drilled shaft under head shear, moment, and axial load: deflection, rotation, bending-moment, shear, and soil-reaction profiles with depth, for free or fixed heads and above-ground stickup.

Methods & theories implemented
  • p–y curve soil models (COM624P / LPILE family): Matlock soft clay, Reese stiff clay above/below water table, Reese (1974) sand (GEC 9's four-segment construction by default, a simplified one on request), API sand, and others.
  • Banded finite-difference beam-column solver with P-Δ (axial-load) effects.
  • Free/fixed head conditions, above-ground stickup, and H-pile strong/weak-axis or concrete-filled-pipe sections.
  • References: Reese, Cox & Koop (1974); Matlock (1970); COM624P; validated against a COM624P oracle suite and the FHWA Micropile LPILE benchmark (V-017).

(1975), stiff clay with free water: GEC 9 p. 219 keeps it for stiff clay exposed to free water at or near the ground surface, and with the groundwater at depth prefers StiffClayAboveWT (Welch & Reese) even below the water table, gamma then submerged; it does not say how near is near, so which of the two a stiff clay below the water table takes is the engineer's call: state it and why, or ask; SoftClayJeanjean {su, gamma, Gmax} (not checked against a print: neither Jeanjean 2009 nor API RP 2GEO is in the reference library; GEC 9's soft clay criterion is SoftClayMatlock); SandReese/SandAPI {phi, gamma, k} where k (kN/m3) is the k of the initial line p = (k z) y: for SandReese GEC 9 Table A-3 gives it by relative density only, loose / medium / dense 5,429 / 16,287 / 33,931 submerged and 6,786 / 24,430 / 61,076 above the water (20 / 60 / 125 and 25 / 90 / 225 lb/in3); for SandAPI API RP 2A Fig. 6.8.7-1 by phi', e.g. phi' 30 / 35 / 40: 9,260 / 22,260 / 42,510 below the water table and 12,650 / 36,970 / 75,270 above; WeakRock {qu, Er}. SandReese also takes optional construction='reese1974' (default: GEC 9 App. A.4's four-segment curve, linear -> parabola -> straight line -> p_u, A and B from Figs. A-10 and A-11) | 'simplified' (the module's own three-part curve, which no held page prints). StiffClayAboveWT with loading='cyclic' also needs n_cycles, N, the number of times the design lateral load is applied (>= 1; the references give no number to assume; Welch & Reese, COM624P Eq. 3.29, y_c = y_s + y50 C log N, so y50 times 1 + 0.6 log10 N). WeakRock (Reese 1997, FHWA GEC 9 App. A.5) also takes optional RQD (%, default 100: alpha_r = 1/3, the printed lower bound; alpha_r rises linearly to 1.0 at RQD 0), krm (default 0.0005, the softer end of 0.00005-0.0005) and rock_top (depth of the rock surface, m; default the top of the weak-rock layers that hold the layer); its gamma_r is accepted and not used (the criterion does not use the unit weight).

Applicability limits & conventions
  • Section stiffness is a linear EI (an uncracked composite section by transformed section) or Branson's cracked EI for reinforced concrete; no moment–curvature analysis. In the micropile benchmark (V-017) the uncracked composite EI gives 3.32 mm against LPILE's 3.3 mm.

4.2.3 pile_group — Pile groups

Problems it solves

How a rigid pile cap distributes structural loads to the individual piles, and how much a group settles: axial/lateral/torsional load sharing under a 6-DOF load set, group efficiency, and group settlement.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Rigid-cap 6-DOF stiffness analysis — per-pile axial and lateral stiffness, batter, and one right-hand sign convention carried end to end.
  • Group efficiency factor ηg read from the printed rows by soil, the cap's contact with the ground and the spacing (GEC-12 Sec. 7.2.2; UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-26 for drilled shafts, CFA, displacement piles and micropiles); block failure by GEC-12 Eqs. 7-36 and 7-37; lateral p-multipliers by row (AASHTO as GEC-12 prints it, or Mokwa, UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-38).
  • Meyerhof (1976) SPT group settlement as GEC-12 Eqs. 7-50 to 7-52 print it, and an elastic equivalent-footing settlement (GEC-12 Sec. 7.3.5.3, 2V:1H spread, to where the stress falls to 10 % of the footing's).
  • References: FHWA GEC-12 Vol. I ch. 7; UFC 3-220-20 ch. 6; validated against GEC-12 Vol. III Tables D-13, D-14 and D-23 and UFC 3-220-20 Appendix B-5.4 (V-005, V-060).

Applicability limits & conventions

4.2.4 drilled_shaft — Drilled shafts

Problems it solves

Axial capacity of a drilled shaft (bored pile) in soil and rock: side resistance in clay and sand, base resistance, rock-socket capacity, belled bases, and the LRFD factored resistance.

Methods & theories implemented
  • α-method side resistance in clay (AASHTO 0.55 default, or the GEC-10 Chen (2011) rational α with the UU/UC→CIUC su transform).
  • β-method side resistance in sand (GEC-10 (2018) Eq. 10-13 by default: Ko from the OCR, σ′p from each layer’s N60; or the O’Neill–Reese depth β by name).
  • Base resistance in sand (0.60·N60 with the large-diameter reduction) and clay (Nc·su cap); rock-socket side + base; permanent-casing and top/bottom exclusion zones.
  • LRFD resistance factors and capacity-vs-depth curves.
  • References: FHWA GEC-10 (FHWA-NHI-18-024); O’Neill & Reese; Chen & Kulhawy; validated against the GEC-10 Appendix A example (V-006/V-007/V-008).

Parameters of drilled_shaft_capacity
ParameterTypeDescription
diameterfloatrequiredShaft diameter (m).
shaft_lengthfloatrequiredShaft length (m). Alias: length.
layersarrayrequiredArray of {thickness, soil_type, unit_weight, cu, phi, N60, qu, RQD} dicts. soil_type: cohesive/cohesionless/rock. A cohesionless layer at the shaft tip needs its N60 (end bearing q_b = 57.5*N60 kPa, GEC-10 Eq. 10-14, N60 the mean of the cohesionless layers' N60 between the base and two base diameters below it, by thickness, limited to 50, p. 10-15; a layer there with no N60, or of cohesive soil or rock, is left out); without it the call is refused. Under beta_method 'rational' (the default, GEC-10 2018 Eq. 10-13) each cohesionless layer the shaft passes through needs its N60 (sigma'p by Eq. 10-11 or 10-12) or a direct OCR, else the call is refused; it also takes N1_60 (overburden-corrected SPT; phi' = 27.5+9.2*log10[(N1)60], GEC-10 Example 10-1 and Eq. A-2, where the layer gives no phi; a phi given is used and the result's choices give the correlation's value beside it), sigma_p_correlation ('clean_sand' default: Eq. 10-11 with m = 0.6, clean quartzitic sands; 'silty_sand': m = 0.8, silty sands to sandy silts; 'gravel': Eq. 10-12, sigma'p/pa = 0.15*N60, gravelly soils; GEC-10 p. 10-11) and sigma_v_ref (kPa, pre-scour effective stress for the OCR; default the layer's own sigma'v). A rock layer's RQD (default 100) sets alpha_E of the side resistance under rock_side_method 'caving' (GEC-10 Table 10-3) and the base under rock_base_method 'rqd'; under the default 'gec10' an RQD below 100 within one base diameter below the base needs rock_base_conditions_met, or the tip rock layer's GSI and m_i. A rock layer also takes GSI (Geological Strength Index of the rock mass, 0 to 100, from the core descriptions; GEC-10 p. 10-23 names GSI, not RMR) and m_i (Hoek-Brown constant of the intact rock, by rock type, GEC 5 Table 9-10, as GEC-10 p. 10-24 points to): with the base in that layer they give GEC-10's base for a fractured rock mass, the Hoek-Brown base, Eqs. 10-24 to 10-29, taken where the rock is not taken to meet the conditions of Eq. 10-23 and shown beside 2.5*qu where it is (see rock_base_conditions_met); a rock layer within one base diameter below the base that gives them has its own Hoek-Brown base among the result's alternatives. GSI or m_i on any other layer (above the base, further below it, or with the base in soil) is refused: nothing would use them; capacity_vs_depth takes them on any layer a trial base is in.
gwt_depthfloatoptionalGroundwater depth (m).
factor_of_safetyfloatoptionalFactor of safety.
beta_methodstroptionalCohesionless side resistance. 'rational' (default) = GEC-10 (2018) Sec. 10.3.5.1, Eqs. 10-5 to 10-13 (pp. 10-10 to 10-12): f_SN = beta*sigma'v on each layer's average sigma'v, beta = (K/Ko)*Ko*tan(phi'), Ko = (1-sin phi')*OCR^(sin phi') <= Kp, OCR = sigma'p/sigma'v, sigma'p from the layer's N60 (Eq. 10-11 or 10-12), beta limited to its value at 7.5 ft, no limit on f_SN; needs each cohesionless layer's N60 or OCR. 'depth' = O'Neill & Reese (1999) beta = 1.5-0.135*sqrt(z, ft) = 1.5-0.245*sqrt(z, m), 0.25-1.2, x N60/15 where N60 < 15, f_s <= 4 ksf = 191.5 kPa (FHWA NHI-06-089 Eqs. 9-41 to 9-43, the limit p. 9-133), which GEC-10 (2018) does not print. allowed: rational, depth
K_over_KofloatoptionalK/Ko in the GEC-10 beta (beta_method 'rational'): 1 = 'a rational first-order approximation', no stress change from construction (GEC-10 p. 10-11); 2/3 or lower 'when these aspects of construction quality are not controlled properly' or soil caving is allowed (p. 10-12). 0 < K_over_Ko <= 1.
top_exclusionfloatoptionalSide resistance left out over the top of the shaft (m), in every layer, when given. Left out: none over the top 1.5 m in cohesive soil, GEC-10's 'top 5 ft' (p. 10-17, printed in Sec. 10.3.5.2 for cohesive soils, 'or to the depth of seasonal moisture change', 'subject to modification based on local experience and judgment of the designer'), and side resistance from the top in cohesionless soil and rock (Secs. 10.3.5.1 and 10.3.5.3 print no such zone; Examples 10-1 and 10-5 take the sand's from the surface, Example 10-4 the socket's over its whole length). Give 1.5 to leave the top 5 ft out of sand and rock too (frost, seasonal moisture, gapping from cyclic lateral load), or the depth of seasonal moisture change. casing_depth, where deeper, takes its place.
bottom_exclusionfloatoptionalSide resistance left out over the bottom of the shaft (m) in cohesive soil. Default 0: GEC-10 (2018) prints no such zone, and Example 10-2 (p. 10-18) takes the clay's side resistance to the base. FHWA NHI-06-089 p. 9-129 (O'Neill & Reese 1999) leaves out the bottom 5 ft (1.524 m), its Fig. 9-49 the bottom one diameter (give the diameter for that).
alpha_methodstroptionalCohesive side resistance. 'rational' (default) = GEC-10 (2018) Sec. 10.3.5.2, Eq. 10-18 (p. 10-16): alpha = 0.30+0.17/(su(CIUC)/pa), f_SN = alpha*su(CIUC), su(CIUC) from cu by su_test_type. 'aashto' = O'Neill & Reese (1999) as FHWA NHI-06-089 Eqs. 9-37a/b print it (p. 9-129): alpha = 0.55 for cu/pa <= 1.5, 0.55-0.1*(cu/pa-1.5) to 2.5, on cu; GEC-10 recommends Eq. 10-18 'as a revision' to it. allowed: rational, aashto
su_test_typestroptionalFor alpha_method 'rational': the lab test each layer's cu came from. 'ciuc' (default) = cu taken as su(CIUC), no transform; 'uc' / 'uu' = transformed to su(CIUC) on the layer's sigma'vo by GEC-10 Eq. 10-16 / 10-17 (Chen & Kulhawy 1993, p. 10-16; Example 10-2 takes a UU strength). The base in clay takes the same su(CIUC) (Example 10-3). allowed: ciuc, uc, uu
clay_base_methodstroptionalBase resistance with the tip in cohesive soil. 'gec10' (default) = GEC-10 (2018) p. 10-19: q_BN = N*c*su (Eq. 10-19), su the mean of the cohesive soil over 2B below the base, by thickness (p. 10-19; the tip layer at its su(CIUC) as its side resistance took it, each clay layer below on its own cu, transformed alike; cohesionless or rock layers within 2B left out; where the profile ends short of 2B, the mean of what it gives, said in the choices), N*c from Table 10-2 by su (6.5 at 500 psf, 8.0 at 1,000 psf, 9.0 at 2,000 psf or more; held at 6.5 below 500 psf), (2/3)[1 + D/(6B)]*N*c*su where the depth D < 3B (Eq. 10-20), no upper limit. 'oneill_reese' = FHWA NHI-06-089 Eqs. 9-39, 9-40 (p. 9-131): Nc = 6[1 + 0.2 z/D] <= 9, x 0.67 where su < 0.5 ksf, q_t <= 80 ksf, on the tip layer's cu. allowed: gec10, oneill_reese
rock_base_methodstroptionalBase resistance with the tip in rock. 'gec10' (default) = GEC-10 (2018) Eq. 10-23 (p. 10-22): q_BN = 2.5*qu, for rock massive or tightly jointed to one diameter below the base, no cavities beneath, a clean base (Example 10-4 takes it with RQD 37 to 100); for a fractured rock mass the Hoek-Brown base, Eqs. 10-24 to 10-29 (pp. 10-23, 10-24; Turner and Ramey 2010): m_b = m_i*exp((GSI-100)/28), s = exp((GSI-100)/9), a = 1/2+(1/6)(exp(-GSI/15)-exp(-20/3)), A = sigma'vb + qu*(m_b*sigma'vb/qu + s)^a, q_BN = A + qu*(m_b*A/qu + s)^a, q_BN/qu limited to 2.5 (p. 10-24), on the tip rock layer's qu, GSI and m_i and the vertical effective stress at the base; resistance factor 0.50 (p. 10-24, Table 8-4); which of the two by rock_base_conditions_met. 'rqd' = q_b/q_u reduced by the tip rock's RQD below 70 (1.5 at 50, 0.8 at 25, 0.4 at 0), cited to GEC-10's 2010 edition, not in the reference library, and not a method GEC-10 Table 8-4 gives a resistance factor for. allowed: gec10, rqd
rock_base_conditions_metbooloptionalFor rock_base_method 'gec10' with the tip in rock: whether the rock below the base meets the three conditions GEC-10 p. 10-22 sets on q_BN = 2.5*qu (massive or tightly jointed, no compressible seams or joints, to at least one diameter below the base; no solution cavities or voids beneath it; a clean base achieved and verified). The engineer's judgment: Example 10-4 takes 2.5 with RQD 37 to 100 because 'Rock coring and local experience indicate the rock mass below the socket tip is competent'. true = 2.5*qu (Eq. 10-23) as stated. false = GEC-10's base for a fractured rock mass, the Hoek-Brown base (Eqs. 10-24 to 10-29), on the tip rock layer's GSI and m_i; refused, naming them, where that layer does not give them. Left out = taken as met, said in the result's choices, where every layer within one base diameter below the base is rock with RQD 100 (the layer default), with the Hoek-Brown base on the tip rock layer's GSI and m_i beside it where they are given; where a layer there has an RQD below 100 or is soil, the Hoek-Brown base on the tip rock layer's GSI and m_i (2.5*qu bounds it above), and the call is refused, naming them, where that layer does not give them.
large_base_reductionbooloptionalO'Neill & Reese's (1999) reduction of base resistance for a large base: 1.27/B in cohesionless soil for a base wider than 1.27 m, F_r = 2.5/(a*B + 2.5*b) <= 1 in cohesive soil for a base wider than 1.90 m (B the bell's where there is one). Default false: GEC-10 (2018) prints neither (Eqs. 10-14, 10-19, 10-20); true applies it.
pafloatoptionalAtmospheric pressure (kPa) for the rational chains.
rock_side_CfloatoptionalC in the rock side resistance f_s = C*pa*sqrt(qu/pa) (GEC-10 Eq. 10-21, p. 10-20). Default 1.0, 'recommended for design of "normal" rock sockets' (pp. 10-20, 10-21; Example 10-4): conventional equipment, nominally clean sidewalls, no caving, no smearing. 0.65 = the value of Eq. 10-22 with alpha_E = 1.0 (rock_side_method 'caving' takes alpha_E from Table 10-3 by RQD). 1.9 for roughened sockets, verified by load tests or local experience (p. 10-22). For rock_side_method 'normal'; refused with 'caving', which takes no C. Needs a rock layer.
rock_side_methodstroptionalRock side resistance. 'normal' (default) = GEC-10 Eq. 10-21, f_s = C*pa*sqrt(qu/pa) with rock_side_C, for a 'normal' socket: conventional equipment, nominally clean sidewalls (pp. 10-20, 10-21). 'caving' = Eq. 10-22 (O'Neill and Reese 1999), f_s = 0.65*alpha_E*pa*sqrt(qu/pa), alpha_E from Table 10-3 (p. 10-21) by each rock layer's RQD and rock_joints (closed joints 1.00, 0.85, 0.60, 0.50, 0.45; open or gouge-filled 0.85, 0.55, 0.55, 0.50, 0.45 at RQD 100, 70, 50, 30, 20 %; linear between the rows, held at 0.45 below RQD 20), for highly fractured or weathered rock that cannot be drilled without artificial support (casing, plug-ahead) or where caving is anticipated. Needs a rock layer. allowed: normal, caving
rock_jointsstroptionalFor rock_side_method 'caving': the joint condition of GEC-10 Table 10-3, 'closed' (default) or 'open' (open or gouge-filled joints), from the cores. allowed: closed, open
socket_diameterfloatoptionalRock socket diameter (m). Defaults to shaft diameter. One diameter for every rock layer: GEC-10 sizes a socket by one diameter B (Eq. 10-21, Example 10-4) and gives none per rock layer. The rock side resistance and, with the tip in rock, the base (pi/4*B^2, GEC-10 Example 10-4, p. 10-28) take it.
bell_diameterfloatoptionalBelled base diameter (m).
casing_depthfloatoptionalPermanent casing depth (m, no side resistance).
fractured_rock_thicknessfloatoptionalDecomposed or fractured rock (m) below the top of the first rock layer that is 'not considered part of the socket for design purposes' (GEC-10 p. 8-15): no rock side resistance over it, while the soil above keeps its own (casing_depth takes both). 0 = all rock is socket. Needs a rock layer.
concrete_fcfloatoptionalCompressive strength f'c of the shaft concrete (kPa; 28 MPa = 28000, at least 1000). The rock side resistance takes qu no higher than it: 'For design, the value of qu used in Equation 10-21 should not exceed the compressive strength of the drilled shaft concrete' (GEC-10 p. 10-21; Example 10-4 gives qu 360 ksf and f'c 576 ksf), in Eq. 10-22 alike. Left out, that limit is not checked and the result's choices say so. No structural check of the shaft is made. Needs a rock layer.

4.2.5 wave_equation — Wave-equation drivability

Problems it solves

Pile drivability and the dynamic bearing check: the bearing graph (static resistance vs blow count), driving stresses, and refusal, from a hammer–cushion–pile–soil model — the analysis behind a driven-pile field acceptance criterion.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Smith (1960) one-dimensional wave-equation model: elasto-plastic soil springs (quake) with smith or smith-viscous damping, hammer/cushion/helmet stack, and a characteristic-line time integration.
  • Single-blow analysis, bearing graph, and drivability vs depth; a hammer database plus custom ram/stroke/efficiency and cushion definitions.
  • References: Smith (1960); GRLWEAP-style modelling; FHWA GEC-12.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • Diesel hammers are an energy→velocity approximation, not a GRLWEAP combustion + ram-cycle model — treat a diesel bearing graph as a trend/limit check, not a tie-out (V-003).

4.2.6 downdrag — Downdrag / neutral plane

Problems it solves

Negative skin friction (downdrag) on a pile through settling ground: the neutral plane, the maximum axial load in the pile, and the drag load added to the structural load.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Neutral plane method — every method the references give, side by side with its neutral plane, drag force and settlement: the intersection of the load and resistance curves at 100 / 50 / 0 % toe mobilization (UFC 3-220-20 §6-7.4, §6-5.8.4.2; GEC-12 §7.3.6.1), the toe resistance compatible with the toe penetration (UFC §6-5.8.4.3), the neutral plane at the bearing layer or at the pile toe, and Endo et al. (1969). The headline is UFC 3-220-20’s §6-7.4 procedure; skin friction on the final effective stress.
  • Fill-induced downdrag, groundwater drawdown, and a maximum-load structural check.
  • References: UFC 3-220-20; FHWA GEC-12; Fellenius; CGPR #56; validated against GEC-12 (V-004, NP/Qmax/DF within 0.2%) and UFC App. B-5.5.

Parameters of downdrag_analysis
ParameterTypeDescription
pile_lengthfloatrequiredPile length (m).
pile_diameterfloatrequiredPile diameter (m).
layersarrayrequiredArray of {thickness, soil_type, unit_weight, phi, cu, beta, alpha, skin_friction_method, soil_class, settling, description} dicts. soil_type must be 'cohesionless' or 'cohesive' (NOT 'sand'/'clay'/'settling_fill'). Skin friction: cohesionless = beta x sigma'v (Beta method, UFC 3-220-20 Eq 6-7), beta as given, else from phi' by GEC-12 Table 7-9 (UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-15, driven piles) for the layer's soil_class ('silt' 0.25-0.50 over 28-34 deg, 'sand' 0.30-0.90 over 32-40 deg, the default, 'gravel' 0.35-0.80 over 35-45 deg), a straight line in phi' between GEC-12 Table 7-9's range ends (the module's reading; the table prints only the ends), held at the ends outside the range; soil_class also picks the toe's Nt row (Nt_method); cohesive = alpha x cu (Alpha method, UFC 3-220-20 Eq 6-8, the default; alpha as given, else read off alpha_chart: UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-16 and Fig 6-14 by default), or with skin_friction_method 'beta' beta x sigma'v for long-term, drained conditions (UFC 3-220-20 6-5.4.1; GEC-12 7.2.1.3.4), beta required (GEC-12 Table 7-9: clay 0.15-0.35; cu then only for a toe in the layer). A cohesive layer takes no phi, and beta only with skin_friction_method 'beta'; a cohesionless layer takes no alpha. Mark settling layers with settling=True; a settling layer also needs its compressibility: cohesionless -> E_s (elastic modulus, kPa, > 0) and optional nu_s; cohesive -> Cc and e0 (optional Cr, sigma_p kPa) or C_ec/C_er.

fill_thicknessfloatoptionalFill thickness causing downdrag (m).
fill_unit_weightfloatoptionalFill unit weight (kN/m3).
gw_drawdownfloatoptionalGroundwater drawdown (m).

allowable_settlementfloatoptionalAllowable pile settlement (m) for the settlement check.
NtfloatoptionalToe bearing capacity factor: R_toe = Nt x sigma'v(toe) x A_toe in cohesionless soil, Nt x cu x A_toe in cohesive. Give the MOBILIZED value -- the toe resistance actually developed at the pile's settlement -- not the ultimate. Omitted, Nt is the ULTIMATE value: 9 in clay (UFC 3-220-20 6-5.4.3.3), and in cohesionless soil from the toe layer's phi' by Nt_method (60-120 in dense sand at 34-38 deg by the default); then the load and resistance curves often do not intersect and the neutral plane is where the pile and soil settle equally, the toe force compatible with the toe penetration (UFC 3-220-20 6-5.8.4.3; see neutral_plane_method). UFC 3-220-20 6-5.8.4.2: check 0 %, 50 % and 100 % toe mobilization.
Nt_methodstringoptionalWhere a cohesionless toe's ultimate Nt comes from when Nt is not given, both UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-17 (p. 421; qb = Nq sigma'zD, Eq 6-20): 'fellenius' (default) = its Fellenius (2021) column, the same values as GEC-12 Table 7-9, by the toe layer's soil_class (silt 20-40 over 28-34 deg, sand 30-150 over 32-40 deg, gravel 60-300 over 35-45 deg), a straight line in phi' between GEC-12 Table 7-9's range ends (the module's reading; the table prints only the ends), held at the ends outside the range; 'cheng' = its equation after Cheng (2004), Nq ~= 1.2 (Z/b)^-0.437 exp[6.34 (Z/b)^0.0486 tan phi'], Z the pile length and b pile_diameter, at most 200 unless project-specific information supports more (give Nt then). The result's choices give the other route's value. allowed: fellenius, cheng
pile_unit_weightfloatoptionalPile material unit weight (kN/m3), times pile_area for the pile's own weight; used only when include_pile_weight is true. Default 78.5 = steel, the same material as the pile_E default (concrete is about 24). For an H or pipe pile give pile_area as the steel area (pile_area defaults to the solid circle).
include_pile_weightbooloptionalWhether the load curve carries the pile's own weight. Default false: left out, as UFC 3-220-20 Fig 6-26 and FHWA GEC-12 7.3.6.1 (and their worked examples) do. True adds the weight of the pile above the neutral plane to Q_np and the drag force.
n_sublayersintoptionalSublayers per soil layer for the depth discretization.
neutral_plane_methodstringoptionalWhich method gives the reported numbers; every method is evaluated and returned in neutral_plane_comparison whatever is chosen. 'auto' (default) = the UFC 3-220-20 6-7.4 procedure: the intersection of the load and resistance curves with the toe at toe_mobilization, or, when they do not intersect, where the pile and soil settle equally with the toe force compatible with the toe penetration (UFC 6-5.8.4.3, Fig 6-19). 'force_equilibrium' (the curves' intersection only; error if they do not intersect); 'settlement_compatibility' (pile and soil settle equally, toe force compatible with the toe penetration); 'bearing_layer_top' (top of the bearing layer, end-bearing pile, UFC 6-7.4 step 5); 'pile_toe' (whole shaft in negative skin friction, upper bound); 'endo' (Endo et al. 1969, CGPR #56 Table 3.1 fraction of the embedment; needs endo_bearing_condition). allowed: auto, force_equilibrium, settlement_compatibility, bearing_layer_top, pile_toe, endo
toe_mobilizationfloatoptionalFraction (0-1) of the nominal toe resistance mobilized where the load and resistance curves intersect. 1.0 = UFC 6-7.4 step 3 full mobilization ('a conservative approach for evaluating the drag force'); 0.5 and 0 = the other UFC 6-5.8.4.2 / GEC-12 7.3.6.1 cases for settlement (all three always reported in the comparison).
endo_bearing_conditionstringoptionalCGPR #56 Table 3.1 condition for Endo et al. (1969). allowed: floating, stiff_flexible, end_bearing
skin_friction_stressstringoptionalEffective stress for Beta-method skin friction (sand, and clay with skin_friction_method 'beta') and the sand toe: 'final' (default; sigma'v0 + fill/drawdown change, as UFC 3-220-20 6-7.4 step 2 requires) or 'initial' (sigma'v0). allowed: final, initial
influence_depth_criterionstringoptionalHow deep below the toe the toe load is counted in the settlement (toe force spread 2V:1H from an equivalent footing as wide as the pile): to where its stress increase falls below 'bearing_stress' (default) = 10% of the bearing stress of the equivalent footing (UFC 3-220-20 6-5.8.4.3; 2.16 pile widths for a single pile) or 'effective_stress' = 10% of the existing vertical effective stress (FHWA GEC-12 Vol I step 1c: 7.3.5.3 for clay below the toe, 7.3.5.6 for sand, 7.3.5.5 for both; deeper for a loaded toe in soft soil). Either way the fill / drawdown, which does not decay with depth, compresses the settling layers below the toe down to the bottom of the soil profile; give the profile down to the base of the compressible soil. allowed: bearing_stress, effective_stress
influence_depth_warning_percentfloatoptionalThe result warns when the two influence_depth_criterion rules (UFC 3-220-20 6-5.8.4.3 and FHWA GEC-12 step 1c) give pile head settlements or drag forces that differ by more than this percentage of the larger of the two (of allowable_settlement / structural_capacity where given), and whenever a settlement or structural check passes with one rule and fails with the other. The rule used is not changed. Default 25 %: the engineer's call, not a reference's figure; neither reference says how far two settlement estimates may differ before it matters.
alpha_chartstringoptionalWhere a cohesive layer's alpha comes from when the layer leaves it out (a given alpha is kept). 'ufc_fig_6_14' (default; UFC 3-220-20 6-5.4.2, pp. 415-417, as its drag example App. B-5.4 reads it): soft clay (su below 800 psf) alpha 1 by Table 6-16; firm to very stiff clay off Fig 6-14 by su/Pa, curve A at Z of 40b or more, curve B at Z = 10b, linear between, Z from the ground surface to the clay's base or the pile toe and b = pile_diameter. 'gec12_fig_7_17': FHWA GEC-12 7.2.1.3.2 Step 1, Ca off Fig. 7-17 by su, D/b and fig_7_17_curve, as drawn (Ca may exceed su). choices states each clay's alpha and where it came from. Refused (with fig_7_17_curve and alpha_transition_zone) where no cohesive layer along the pile leaves alpha out. allowed: ufc_fig_6_14, gec12_fig_7_17
fig_7_17_curvestringoptionalWith alpha_chart 'gec12_fig_7_17' only, and then required where a clay leaves alpha out: the Fig. 7-17 curves for the pile, 'concrete_timber_corrugated' (concrete, timber or corrugated steel; an H-pile takes the corrugated curve, GEC-12 p. 247) or 'smooth_steel'. allowed: concrete_timber_corrugated, smooth_steel
alpha_transition_zonebooloptionalWhether the top 10 pile widths of a stiff or very stiff clay (su 1500 psf or more) directly under soft clay take UFC 3-220-20 Eq 6-9, alpha = 0.28 (su/Pa)^-0.44 with the unit side resistance at least the soft clay's, and under sand alpha 1.0 (pp. 416-417, as App. B-5.4 does). Left out: true with alpha_chart 'ufc_fig_6_14', false with 'gec12_fig_7_17'. Applies only where the stiff clay's alpha is left out; refused where no such clay lies under soft clay or sand. The zone runs 10 pile widths from the top of the stiff clay however it is split into layers.
ground_elevationfloatoptionalElevation of the ground surface the depths are measured from (m): the top of the layers, where the pile head is taken (the original ground under a fill). Figures only: the calc package's profiles are drawn against elevation; every result stays in depth and no number changes.
Worked example

Ask → A 0.4 m pile, 18 m long, through settling fill and soft clay over sand, with a 400 kN dead load. Where is the neutral plane and how large is the drag load?

call_agent(
    agent_name='downdrag',
    method='downdrag_analysis',
    parameters={
        "pile_length": 18.0,
        "pile_diameter": 0.4,
        "layers": [
                {
                        "thickness": 6.0,
                        "soil_type": "cohesive",
                        "unit_weight": 17.0,
                        "cu": 30.0,
                        "Cc": 0.3,
                        "e0": 1.0,
                        "settling": true
                },
                {
                        "thickness": 14.0,
                        "soil_type": "cohesionless",
                        "unit_weight": 19.0,
                        "phi": 34.0,
                        "settling": false
                }
        ],
        "Q_dead": 400.0,
        "fill_thickness": 2.0,
        "fill_unit_weight": 19.0,
        "gwt_depth": 3.0
    },
)

Applicability limits & conventions
  • For an H-pile the box toe area must be passed as the pile area; the module’s intrinsic β-shaft can differ from a Nordlund shaft, so feed the design distribution to isolate the neutral-plane equilibrium.

4.3 Earth retention & excavation support

Walls that hold back soil and the systems that keep an excavation open and stable.

4.3.1 sheet_pile — Sheet-pile walls

Problems it solves

Cantilever and single-anchor flexible retaining walls: the embedment for stability, the maximum bending moment, and the anchor force, from a layered earth-pressure diagram with groundwater.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Rankine / Coulomb active and passive coefficients (with wall friction), and a Caquot–Kerisel log-spiral passive option that avoids Coulomb’s over-prediction at high δ.
  • Free-earth-support solution for cantilever and anchored walls; layered active-pressure builder with hydrostatic water; embedment-increase factor and a FOS on passive resistance.
  • References: Rankine; Coulomb; Caquot–Kerisel; NAVFAC DM7.2; validated against Caltrans T&S Ex 7-2 / 8-1 (V-025/V-013) and, for the anchored wall’s maximum moment, the USS Steel Sheet Piling Design Manual’s Design Example No. 2 (within 1 %).
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Sheet Pile
MethodWhat it doesParams
cantilever_wallCantilever sheet pile wall: embedment depth and maximum moment.9
anchored_wallAnchored sheet pile wall: embedment, anchor force, and moment.9
Parameters of cantilever_wall
ParameterTypeDescription
excavation_depthfloatrequiredExcavation depth (m).
layersarrayrequiredArray of soil-layer dicts, top down: {thickness (m, required), unit_weight (kN/m3, required; alias gamma), friction_angle (deg, default 30; alias phi), cohesion (kPa, default 0), wall_friction_deg (deg, 0 to friction_angle; alias delta), interface_soil (the soil against the steel, a row of the steel sheet pile wall friction table printed in UFC 3-220-20 Table 4-1, p. 184, EM 1110-2-2504 Table 3-3, p. 3-4, and the USS Steel Sheet Piling Design Manual Table 4, p. 13: 'clean_gravel' 22 deg (clean gravel, gravel-sand mixtures, well-graded rock fill with spalls), 'clean_sand' 17 (clean sand, silty sand-gravel mixture, single size hard rock fill), 'silty_sand' 14 (silty sand, gravel or sand mixed with silt or clay), 'fine_sandy_silt' 11 (fine sandy silt, nonplastic silt); at most friction_angle; not with wall_friction_deg)}. wall_friction_deg or interface_soil is used on both sides by pressure_method 'coulomb' and 'log_spiral'. A layer giving neither takes, with 'log_spiral', the clean_sand row (17 deg, at most its phi') on the passive side when it has no cohesion and no wall friction on the active side or in a layer with cohesion (UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-37 step 1, p. 237: 'Passive pressures for clean coarse grained soils include wall friction (see Table 4-1)'; it ignores wall friction in other soils, so give wall_friction_deg 0 in a silty sand or silt); with 'coulomb' none (UFC 3-220-20 p. 190: passive pressure 'should be calculated using the log spiral method and not the Coulomb method'). The result's choices give each layer's wall friction and its Kp at the other rows and at delta = 0, and where a layer took the clean sand row by default the embedment with none.
surchargefloatoptionalSurface surcharge (kPa).
FOS_passivefloatoptionalFOS applied to passive resistance.
gwt_depth_activefloatoptionalGroundwater depth on active (retained) side (m).
gwt_depth_passivefloatoptionalGroundwater depth on passive (excavated) side (m).
pressure_methodstroptionalEarth pressure theory. 'log_spiral' uses Coulomb active + the log-spiral PASSIVE coefficient from log_spiral_source (avoids Coulomb's over-prediction of Kp at high delta/phi). 'coulomb' and 'log_spiral' take each layer's wall friction (layers: wall_friction_deg or interface_soil; what a layer giving neither takes is in the layers description). allowed: rankine, coulomb, log_spiral
log_spiral_sourcestroptionalWith pressure_method 'log_spiral', the printed source of the passive Kp. 'ufc_3_220_20' (default): UFC 3-220-20 (DM 7.2), the source the wall's geometry calls for (pp. 191-193); a sheet pile has a vertical face and the tool takes level ground in front of it, so that is Eq. 4-12 (p. 191), at each layer's wall_friction_deg. 'caquot_kerisel_1948': the Caquot and Kerisel (1948) chart, Kp at delta = phi times the printed reduction factor R(delta/phi), Caltrans Trenching and Shoring Manual Fig. 4-20 (p. 4-30), the method its Sec. 4-6 uses for passive pressure. 'dm7_2_fig_4_12', 'dm7_2_fig_4_13': UFC 3-220-20 Figs. 4-12 (p. 192, theta = 0 curve) and 4-13 (p. 193, beta = 0 row), Kerisel and Absi (1990), drawn for delta/phi' = 0.66 only, so every layer's wall_friction_deg must be 0.66 x its friction_angle; UFC 3-220-20 p. 260 says Kp for a tied-back wall 'should be obtained from Figure 4-12'. 'dm7_2_eq_4_12': Eq. 4-12 by name. They differ: at phi 30, delta/phi 0.66 the 1948 chart gives 5.4, the UFC charts 5.3 and Eq. 4-12 5.1. UFC 3-220-20 footnote 21 (p. 191): the 1982 DM 7.2 charts 'used delta/phi' = 1 along with reduction ratios', which 'were averages that introduced substantial inaccuracy for some cases'; the 1948 chart takes that form (Kp at delta = phi times R). UFC 3-220-20 Table 4-2 (p. 194) is not used: the log-spiral Kp in its row headed delta/phi' = 0.5, 5.3, 8.0, 12 and 20 at phi' = 30, 35, 40 and 45, are Fig. 4-13's values, drawn for delta/phi' = 0.66 (5.30, 8.00, 12.0, 20), and the Coulomb Kp printed beside them, 6.1, 9.8, 18 and 44, are Coulomb's at delta = 0.66 phi' (at 0.5 it gives 5.0, 7.4, 11.8 and 21.4). Eq. 4-12 at delta/phi' = 0.5 gives 4.46, 6.33, 9.33 and 14.3. The tool reads Fig. 4-13 at the 0.66 it is drawn for and Eq. 4-12 at the wall friction given. The result's choices give each layer's Kp from the source used and from the others. allowed: ufc_3_220_20, caquot_kerisel_1948, dm7_2_eq_4_12, dm7_2_fig_4_12, dm7_2_fig_4_13
embedment_increasefloatoptionalMultiplier on the computed embedment (e.g. 1.2 for the traditional 20% rule). Use 1.0 (default) when FOS_passive already provides the safety basis — do not double-count.
Worked example

Ask → A cantilever sheet pile retains a 4 m excavation in sand (φ=32°) with a 10 kPa surcharge. What embedment is needed and what is the maximum moment?

call_agent(
    agent_name='sheet_pile',
    method='cantilever_wall',
    parameters={

        "layers": [
                {
                        "thickness": 15.0,
                        "unit_weight": 18.0,
                        "friction_angle": 32.0,
                        "cohesion": 0.0
                }
        ],
        "surcharge": 10.0,
        "FOS_passive": 1.5,
        "embedment_increase": 1.2
    },
)

Applicability limits & conventions
  • analyze_cantilever is a continuous per-metre free-earth-support solver — soldier-pile effective-width/arching and the simplified toe-moment cubic are not modelled (V-012).

4.3.2 soe — Support of excavation

Problems it solves

Support of an open excavation: braced and cantilever walls, apparent-pressure diagrams, strut/anchor loads, wall-section selection, and the bottom-stability checks (basal heave, blowout, piping).

Methods & theories implemented
  • FHWA apparent-pressure envelopes (Terzaghi–Peck / Peck) for braced cuts and anchored walls, with tributary strut/anchor loads and hinge moments.
  • Cantilever and single-anchor free-earth solutions; ground-anchor design; wall-section sizing.
  • Basal heave — Bjerrum–Eide bearing ratio and a Caltrans force balance with sidewall shear; bottom blowout and piping (exit-gradient) checks.
  • References: FHWA GEC-4 (FHWA-IF-99-015); Terzaghi & Peck; Bjerrum & Eide; Caltrans T&S; validated V-014/V-016.

Parameters of braced_excavation
ParameterTypeDescription
excavation_depthfloatrequiredExcavation depth (m).
layersarrayrequiredArray of soil-layer dicts, top down: {thickness (m, required), unit_weight (kN/m3, required), friction_angle (deg, default 30), cohesion (kPa, default 0), soil_type ('sand' or 'clay', also 'soft_clay' or 'stiff_clay'; REQUIRED on each layer above the excavation base, refused if missing)}. soil_type picks the Terzaghi-Peck apparent-pressure envelope: the one for sands where sand is the thicker over the excavation depth, else the one for clays, soft to medium or stiff fissured by the average N = gamma*H/cu over the excavation depth (> 4 soft). The embedment below the excavation uses each layer's own phi and c. The last layer continues below its thickness.
supportsarrayoptionalSupport levels [{depth (m), support_type ('strut' or 'anchor'), spacing (m), angle_deg}].
surchargefloatoptionalSurface surcharge (kPa); added to the envelope as Ka*q (sand) or q (clay).
gwt_depthfloatoptionalGroundwater depth behind the wall (m); water pressure is added for sand envelopes.
gwt_depth_excavationfloatoptionalGroundwater depth on the excavation side (m from top of wall), never above the excavation base. Default: same as gwt_depth.
FOS_passivefloatoptionalEmbedment FS, MR = FS*MD about the lowest support (Caltrans uses 1.3).
embedment_increasefloatoptionalMultiplier on the free-earth-support embedment.
passive_theorystroptionalThe passive coefficient below the excavation: 'rankine' (default) = Rankine's Kp, no wall friction, as the Caltrans Trenching and Shoring Manual's examples take it where the wall friction is zero (pp. 7-18, 7-27), with its note that Rankine 'tends to underestimate the passive earth pressure' and Sec. 4-6 (p. 4-28): Rankine 'should not be used ... because it does not account for wall friction'; 'log_spiral' (or 'caquot_kerisel', the same) = the log-spiral Kp of log_spiral_source at passive_wall_friction_deg in each layer below the excavation. Choices give the other theory's Kp and embedment. allowed: rankine, log_spiral, caquot_kerisel
log_spiral_sourcestroptionalWith passive_theory 'log_spiral', the printed source of Kp, as earth_pressure_coefficient takes it: 'ufc_3_220_20' (default) = UFC 3-220-20 Eq. 4-12 (p. 191), its log-spiral Kp for a vertical face and level ground at any wall friction; 'caquot_kerisel_1948' = the Caltrans Trenching and Shoring Manual Fig. 4-20 chart (its Example 8-1), and 'dm7_2_eq_4_12' = UFC Eq. 4-12 by name, both needing passive_wall_friction_deg given; 'dm7_2_fig_4_12' / 'dm7_2_fig_4_13' = UFC's charts, drawn for delta/phi' 0.66 only. allowed: ufc_3_220_20, caquot_kerisel_1948, dm7_2_eq_4_12, dm7_2_fig_4_12, dm7_2_fig_4_13
passive_wall_friction_degfloatoptionalWith passive_theory 'log_spiral', the wall friction delta (deg) in every layer below the excavation, at most its phi': the engineer's call (UFC 3-220-20 Table 4-1, p. 184; Caltrans Example 8-1 takes 15 deg on phi 30). Left out: delta/phi' = 0.66 (UFC p. 191, 'a common assumption') in a layer without cohesion, none in a layer with cohesion (UFC Fig. 4-37 step 1, p. 237: 'Passive pressures for clean coarse grained soils include wall friction'; in other soils it ignores wall friction); refused with 'caquot_kerisel_1948' or 'dm7_2_eq_4_12', which need it given (Caltrans p. 4-29: 'Given delta'). For soldier piles in coarse-grained soil UFC p. 249 takes KP 'without wall friction': give 0.
FyfloatoptionalSteel yield strength (MPa) for section sizing.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • The single-anchor FHWA apparent-diagram embedment solver and a multi-anchor apparent-envelope helper are documented gaps; the primitives (K, pe, tributary loads, hinge moments) reproduce the worked examples (V-016).
  • Where no moment balance exists within six times the excavation depth, the free-earth solution returns no embedment (and nothing computed from it) with a plain note, never a depth without a solution.

4.3.3 retaining_walls — Retaining walls (cantilever & MSE)

Problems it solves

Gravity/cantilever concrete retaining walls and mechanically-stabilized-earth (MSE) walls: external stability (sliding, overturning, bearing, eccentricity) and MSE internal stability (reinforcement tension and pullout), by ASD and LRFD.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Cantilever-wall stability with Rankine/Coulomb thrust decomposition and Meyerhof bearing.
  • MSE coherent-gravity method: external stability and internal Kr/Ka and F* pullout curves for ribbed strips and steel bar-mats/welded grids.
  • AASHTO/GEC-11 LRFD external stability — Strength I max/min + Service I load-factor combinations, live-load exclusions, and per-mode capacity/demand ratios.
  • References: FHWA GEC-11 (FHWA-NHI-10-025); AASHTO LRFD; validated against GEC-11 Ex E4/E7 (V-009/V-010/V-011).

'back' (default): the front face vertical, the backfill over the battered back counted as resisting weight. 'front': the back face vertical, as UFC 3-220-20 App. B-1 Fig. B-2 (p. 598) and FHWA NHI-06-089 Fig. 10-16(a) and Example 10-3 (p. 10-52) draw it. allowed: back, front
