Deeper, the soil over the toe counts as resisting weight (UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-27, p. 220: 'Weight includes ... weight of soil above footing'; App. B-1.3, p. 599), at gamma_foundation, and include_passive's passive resistance acts over Df.
has_shear_keybooloptionalInclude a shear key below the base (with key_depth). It acts only with include_passive: the sliding check then takes the passive resistance over the depth of the key only, from the underside of the base (depth embedment_depth below the ground in front) to the bottom of the key (embedment_depth + key_depth), the trapezoid UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-29 draws below the toe (p. 224: 'the passive pressure is applied only along the depth of the key and not along the entire burial depth of the wall'; GEC-6 Fig. 5-22 likewise), in place of the passive over the embedment; with the undrained rule it counts cu, as GEC-6 Eq. 5-41 (p. 101) counts Pp in front of the key. GEC-6 Sec. 5.4 (pp. 100-101): keys in granular soils 'are not very efficient in developing passive pressures'; its key method is for stiff, overconsolidated clays and soft rock. UFC: 'it is also prudent to consider some amount of future excavation in front of the wall'.
key_depthfloatoptionalShear key depth below the underside of the base slab (m).
surchargefloatoptionalUniform LIVE-load surcharge on the backfill (kPa), e.g. traffic. Its thrust K*q*H drives every check. Over the heel it is NOT a resisting force in sliding, overturning or the eccentricity check by default (live_load_resists), and it does load the base in the bearing pressures (surcharge_in_bearing). A pavement or slab is not a surcharge here: model it as retained soil up to the ground surface (it then rests on the heel and resists like the backfill). Any other surcharge is transient live load: its thrust counts in every check, but its weight over the heel does not resist sliding or overturning. A permanent load you want carried as a surcharge goes in dead_load_surcharge.
dead_load_surchargefloatoptionalUniform DEAD-load (permanent) surcharge on the backfill (kPa), a permanent load that is not part of the retained soil (FHWA NHI-06-089 Sec. 10.4.2). Pavements and slabs are normally modelled as retained soil up to the ground surface instead. Its thrust drives every check, added to the live load's. Over the heel it is not a resisting force by default (dead_load_resists=true counts it as resisting weight in sliding and overturning); it loads the base in the bearing pressures (surcharge_in_bearing).
live_load_resistsbooloptionalCount the live-load surcharge over the heel (and its share of a sloped or Coulomb thrust's vertical component) as a resisting force in sliding, overturning and the eccentricity check. Default false: FHWA NHI-06-089 Sec. 10.5.5 (p. 10-43), 'the live load surcharge is not considered as a stabilizing force over the heel of the wall when sliding resistance is being checked'; UFC 3-220-20 App. B-1.2 (p. 597), 'For overturning and sliding checks, it is assumed that the traffic pressure does not act over the wall heel'. true = the free body with the load over the heel, which none of these references uses for a live load. The result's choices say which was used.
dead_load_resistsbooloptionalCount the dead-load surcharge over the heel as a resisting force in sliding, overturning and the eccentricity check. Default false: FHWA NHI-06-089 Sec. 10.5.3 (p. 10-41), for CIP semi-gravity walls the surcharge loads are 'conservatively neglected within the width of the base slab since they contribute to overturning and sliding resistance'. true = counted as a permanent load: GEC-11 Vol I p. 4-22 (AASHTO), loads that increase sliding resistance are included 'only if those loads are permanent'.
surcharge_in_bearingbooloptionalCount the surcharges over the heel in the bearing pressures (q_toe, q_heel, FOS_bearing). Default true: UFC 3-220-20 App. B-1.6 (p. 602), 'it is conservative to include the surcharge over the heel of the wall, if this is possible to occur, in the bearing capacity check'; GEC-11 Vol I p. 4-26. false = the surcharge taken as located behind the heel (NHI-06-089 p. 10-41).
backfill_slopefloatoptionalBackfill slope angle (degrees), rising away from the wall. A backfill descending away from the wall (below 0) is refused.
c_backfillfloatoptionalBackfill cohesion (kPa). The active pressure Ka sigma_v - 2 c sqrt(Ka) is taken as zero where it is negative, the tension zone (UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-5 Note A; FHWA NHI-06-089 p. 10-15); the result's choices give the thrust with c neglected and with NHI's minimum active pressure of 5z kN/m2 beside it.
phi_foundationfloatoptionalFoundation soil friction angle (deg), FULL value — the sliding check applies delta_b = (2/3)*phi_foundation INTERNALLY. Do NOT pre-reduce (passing 2/3*phi here double-counts the reduction). To set the base friction angle directly, use delta_base instead. Defaults to phi_backfill. phi_foundation = 0 gives an undrained strength (c_foundation = cu): sliding_cohesion then defaults to 'undrained'.
c_foundationfloatoptionalFoundation soil cohesion (kPa), FULL value, no 2/3 factor. The sliding check counts it by sliding_cohesion: NOT at all with 'drained' (the default unless phi_foundation is 0), as the undrained shear strength cu with 'undrained' (ca = cu) or 'friction_plus_adhesion' (Ca from UFC 3-220-20 Table 4-1). To set the adhesion directly, use base_adhesion.
sliding_cohesionstroptionalHow the sliding check counts the foundation soil's cohesion, by the rule a reference prints. Default depends on phi_foundation: 'undrained' when phi_foundation is 0 (c_foundation is then cu), else 'drained'. 'drained': R = V tan delta_b, c_foundation NOT counted (GEC-6 Sec. 5.4 Eq. 5-38, p. 100: 'Equations 5-38 and 5-39 should not be combined for use at the same time'; EN 1997-1 6.5.3(10): 'Any effective cohesion c' should be neglected'). 'undrained': R = ca B alone, no friction, ca = c_foundation taken as the undrained shear strength cu, or base_adhesion (GEC-6 Eq. 5-39: 'ca is typically taken as equal to the undrained shear strength'). 'friction_plus_adhesion': R = V tan delta_b + Ca Be, Ca from UFC 3-220-20 Table 4-1 (p. 184) at c_foundation taken as the undrained shear strength (up to 191.5 kPa), or base_adhesion; Be = B - 2e, the effective base width (UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-27 and Sec. 4-5.1.3, p. 223, which adds that the minimum FS 'may also need to be increased when base adhesion is included'). The result's choices give the rule used, its basis and each other rule's FOS_sliding on the same wall. allowed: drained, undrained, friction_plus_adhesion
delta_basefloatoptionalBase interface friction angle delta_b (deg), used DIRECTLY in the sliding check with NO 2/3 factor. Overrides the (2/3)*phi_foundation default. delta_b = phi_foundation for concrete cast against the ground (GEC-6 Sec. 5.4, p. 99: tan delta 'will be equal to the tangent of the friction angle (tan phi) for the soil supporting the footing'). The result's choices state the delta_b used, its basis and the other reading. Refused with sliding_cohesion 'undrained', which counts no friction.
base_adhesionfloatoptionalBase adhesion ca (kPa), used DIRECTLY with sliding_cohesion 'undrained' (in place of cu) or 'friction_plus_adhesion' (in place of the UFC 3-220-20 Table 4-1 value). Refused with 'drained', which counts no adhesion: give sliding_cohesion with it.
include_passivebooloptionalInclude passive resistance in front of the wall in the sliding check (Rankine's Kp unless passive_theory says otherwise; UFC 3-220-20 p. 219: 'typically ignored', and with it considered FSL >= 2.0, Fig. 4-27, so FOS_sliding_required then defaults to 2.0), acting over the embedment, from the ground in front to the underside of the base (embedment_depth, default the base thickness), or with has_shear_key over the depth of the key only (from embedment_depth to embedment_depth + key_depth below the ground in front, UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-29). With the undrained rule it counts the foundation's cu, Kp sigma_v + 2 cu sqrt(Kp) (UFC 3-220-20 Eq. 4-7, p. 178, and p. 181); with the other rules c_foundation is not counted in it (p. 179).
gamma_foundationfloatoptionalFoundation soil unit weight (kN/m3): the passive resistance in front of the wall and the soil over the toe (embedment_depth below the top of the base). Defaults to gamma_backfill.
passive_theorystroptionalWith include_passive, the passive coefficient in front of the wall: 'rankine' (default) = Rankine's Kp, no wall friction; 'log_spiral' (or 'caquot_kerisel', the same) = the log-spiral Kp of log_spiral_source at passive_wall_friction_deg. UFC 3-220-20 (Sec. 4-5.1, Figs. 4-27 and 4-29, pp. 219-224) names no theory for it; choices give the other theory's Kp and FOS_sliding and the FOS with no passive. allowed: rankine, log_spiral, caquot_kerisel
log_spiral_sourcestroptionalWith passive_theory 'log_spiral', the printed source of Kp, as earth_pressure_coefficient takes it: 'ufc_3_220_20' (default) = UFC 3-220-20 Eq. 4-12 (p. 191), its log-spiral Kp for a vertical face and level ground at any wall friction; 'caquot_kerisel_1948' = the Caltrans Trenching and Shoring Manual Fig. 4-20 chart, and 'dm7_2_eq_4_12' = UFC Eq. 4-12 by name, both needing passive_wall_friction_deg given; 'dm7_2_fig_4_12' / 'dm7_2_fig_4_13' = UFC's charts, drawn for delta/phi' 0.66 only. allowed: ufc_3_220_20, caquot_kerisel_1948, dm7_2_eq_4_12, dm7_2_fig_4_12, dm7_2_fig_4_13
passive_wall_friction_degfloatoptionalWith passive_theory 'log_spiral', the wall friction delta in front of the wall (deg), 0 to phi_foundation: the engineer's call (UFC 3-220-20 Table 4-1, p. 184). Left out: delta/phi' = 0.66 (UFC p. 191, 'a common assumption'); refused with 'caquot_kerisel_1948' or 'dm7_2_eq_4_12', which need it given (Caltrans p. 4-29: 'Given delta').
q_allowablefloatoptionalAllowable bearing pressure (kPa) for the bearing check. On soil (bearing_pressure 'uniform', the default) it is compared with q_eq = V/(B - 2e), the uniform pressure over the effective width B' = B - 2e, so give the allowable bearing pressure for B' (GEC-6 Sec. 6.4.2, p. 119: 'Bf in Equation 5-14 may be replaced by B'f'); with 'linear' (the default with founded_on_rock), with the larger edge pressure. Without it the bearing check is NOT RUN: FOS_bearing and passes_bearing are null and checks_not_run lists 'bearing' (q_toe / q_heel are still reported).
gamma_concretefloatoptionalConcrete unit weight (kN/m3). Default 23.6, 150 pcf, as UFC 3-220-20 App. B-1.3 (p. 599) and FHWA NHI-06-089 Example 10-3 (p. 10-53) take it.
FOS_sliding_requiredfloatoptionalRequired sliding FOS; the check passes at or above it. Default depends on include_passive: 1.5 (GEC-6 Eq. 5-40, p. 100; UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-27; FHWA NHI-06-089 Fig. 10-17), 2.0 with the passive resistance counted (UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-27, p. 220, and Sec. 4-5.1.3, p. 223: 'If passive resistance is included, the minimum FSL should be increased to 2.0'). The result's choices say which was taken.
FOS_overturning_requiredfloatoptionalRequired overturning FOS; the check passes at or above it. Default depends on founded_on_rock: 2.0 on soil, 1.5 on rock (FHWA NHI-06-089 Sec. 10.5.5, p. 10-44: 'approximately of 2.0 for soils and 1.5 for rocks'; GEC-6 Sec. 7.3, p. 124: 'greater than about 2.0 for permanent dead loads'). UFC 3-220-20 Sec. 4-5.1.2 (p. 223) asks FOT >= 1.5 for any wall.
pressure_methodstroptionalEarth pressure theory. The active thrust acts on the vertical plane through the back of the heel. 'rankine' (default): the thrust parallel to the backfill slope. 'coulomb': Coulomb's Ka (UFC 3-220-20 Eq. 4-10) at the wall friction on that plane, wall_friction_deg, by default the backfill slope (FHWA NHI-06-089 p. 10-20 and Example 10-3; delta = 0 behind level backfill). At that default Coulomb's Ka on a vertical plane is Rankine's (sloped) Ka, the same thrust (NHI Example 10-3's 0.35 at phi 30, beta 10 is both), so 'coulomb' changes the result only with wall_friction_deg given. allowed: rankine, coulomb
wall_friction_degfloatoptionalWall friction delta on the vertical plane through the back of the heel (deg), with pressure_method 'coulomb', 0 to phi_backfill. Left out: the backfill slope (FHWA NHI-06-089 p. 10-20: on that plane 'there is soil-to-soil contact ... it is generally conservative to assume that the earth pressure is parallel to the slope of the backfill'). Refused with 'rankine'. The result's choices give the delta used and the other reading's Ka.
interface_gap_possiblebooloptionalWhether water or air can reach the base-clay interface. With sliding_cohesion 'undrained' (an undrained clay under the base) the base resistance is then held to 0.4 V (EN 1997-1 Sec. 6.5.3(12)P, Eq. 6.5, p. 65). GEC-6 and UFC 3-220-20 print no such limit. Refused with the other rules. The result's choices give FOS_sliding under the other reading.
founded_on_rockbooloptionalWhether the wall is founded on rock. On rock the eccentricity limit is B/4, the middle half, in place of B/6 (GEC-6 Sec. 6.4.1, p. 119; UFC 3-220-20 Sec. 4-5.1.2, p. 223; FHWA NHI-06-089 Fig. 10-17), FOS_overturning_required defaults to 1.5 and bearing_pressure to 'linear'.
bearing_pressurestroptionalThe bearing pressure compared with q_allowable. Default depends on founded_on_rock: 'uniform' on soil, 'linear' on rock. 'uniform' (the default on soil): q_eq = V / B', B' = B - 2e (GEC-6 Eq. 6-6 and Sec. 6.4.2, p. 119; FHWA NHI-06-089 Fig. 10-17: 'Use uniform stress, qeq, for soils'; UFC 3-220-20 Eq. 4-27 and Sec. 4-5.1.4, p. 224, for soil that is 'relatively ductile'). 'linear' (the default with founded_on_rock): the larger edge pressure of the trapezoid or triangle, q_toe or q_heel (UFC Sec. 4-5.1.4: 'For more brittle materials, such as rock and sensitive clays'; FHWA NHI-06-089 Fig. 10-17). The result's choices give the other pressure's FOS_bearing. allowed: uniform, linear
Worked example

Ask → A 6 m cantilever retaining wall on φ=32° backfill with a 12 kPa surcharge — check sliding, overturning, and bearing.

call_agent(
    agent_name='retaining_walls',
    method='cantilever_wall',
    parameters={
        "wall_height": 6.0,
        "gamma_backfill": 18.0,
        "phi_backfill": 32.0,
        "surcharge": 12.0,
        "q_allowable": 250.0
    },
)

verdict: FAILS: sliding (FOS 1.14 < 1.50 required). Passes: overturning (FOS 2.69 >= 2.00 required); bearing (q_eq 142.8 kPa <= q_allowable 250.0 kPa, FOS 1.75); eccentricity (resultant within the middle third: e = 0.537 m <= B/6 = 0.600 m).
checks_failed: [1 entries]
checks_not_run: [0 entries]

FOS_bearing: 1.751

Here the auto-sized base fails sliding (FOS 1.27 < 1.5) — exactly the kind of check-and-revise loop the toolkit is built for.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • MSE external stability is available both as an ASD factor-of-safety path (default, unchanged) and the packaged LRFD CDR path via lrfd_external=True.

4.3.4 ground_improvement — Ground improvement

Problems it solves

Improving weak ground before it is loaded: aggregate piers and stone columns, prefabricated vertical (wick) drains, surcharge preloading, and vibro-compaction — the settlement reduction, capacity increase, and time to consolidate.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Aggregate piers / stone columns: area-replacement ratio, equal-strain settlement-reduction factor, composite modulus, and the settlement ratio off GEC-13 Fig. 5-21 (weighted modulus, Balaam, and the Priebe curve as GEC-13 prints it, φ = 37.5°; no Priebe formula).
  • Radial consolidation for PVDs by GEC-13 Eq. 2-1, F(n) = ln(n) − 0.75, a 2.5 in drain and smear ignored by default (GEC-13 p. 2-35; smear optional by UFC 3-220-10 Eq. 5-25; well resistance not modelled, GEC-13 p. 2-36), combined with vertical drainage by Carrillo (UFC 3-220-10 Eq. 5-27); drain-spacing design.
  • Surcharge preloading; vibro-compaction feasibility by GEC-13's fines limits (p. 4-65) and SPT N (Table 4-8), with the probe spacing for a target relative density off GEC-13 Fig. 4-34.
  • References: FHWA GEC-13 (ground-modification manual); UFC 3-220-10 (2026); validated V-018/V-019/V-020.
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Aggregate Piers
MethodWhat it doesParams
aggregate_piersAggregate pier (stone column) design: settlement reduction, capacity increase.10
priebe_improvement_factorStone columns: the settlement ratio off the Priebe curve GEC-13 prints, Fig. 5-21 curve (4), phi = 37.5 deg (p. 5-36), which GEC-13 calls the upper bound, for preliminary estimates (p. 5-37).1
General
MethodWhat it doesParams
feasibilityGround improvement method feasibility screening.13
Surcharge
MethodWhat it doesParams

Vibro Compaction
MethodWhat it doesParams
vibro_compactionVibro compaction (vibroflotation) feasibility by GEC-13 Ch. 4 (fines content, SPT N by Table 4-8), and the probe spacing for a target relative density off GEC-13 Fig. 4-34.4
Wick Drains
MethodWhat it doesParams
wick_drainsPrefabricated vertical drain (PVD) consolidation: radial by GEC-13 Eq. 2-1 with F(n) = ln(n) - 0.75 (Eq. 2-2), well resistance not modelled (GEC-13 p. 2-36: 'rarely significant'), combined with vertical drainage by Carrillo (UFC 3-220-10 Eq. 5-27).10
design_drain_spacingFind required drain spacing for a target combined (vertical and radial) consolidation in a target time, by GEC-13 Eq. 2-1 and Carrillo (UFC 3-220-10 Eq. 5-27). GEC-13 p. 2-33 gives typical spacings of 3 to 5 ft in homogeneous clays, 4 to 6 ft in silty clays, 5 to 6.5 ft in coarser soils for about 90 percent consolidation in 3 to 4 months.10
Parameters of aggregate_piers
ParameterTypeDescription
column_diameterfloatrequiredPier column diameter (m).
spacingfloatrequiredCenter-to-center spacing (m). Alternatively give area_replacement_ratio (As/A, 0.1-0.35 typical) and spacing is back-calculated.
area_replacement_ratiofloatoptionalArea replacement ratio As/A (0.1-0.35 typical). Used to compute spacing when spacing is not given.
patternstroptionalInstallation pattern. allowed: triangular, square
E_soilfloatoptionalSurrounding soil modulus (kPa). With settlement_method 'stress_ratio', used only for the composite modulus E_comp = E_soil*[1 + as*(n-1)]; the GEC-13 Fig. 5-21 methods need it given, for E_c/E_s.
nfloatoptionalStress concentration ratio sigma_c/sigma_s; sets the improved bearing and, with settlement_method 'stress_ratio', the settlement reduction factor. GEC-13 for stone columns: measured 'between 2.0 and 5.0' (p. 5-31), and 'For preliminary design, a ratio of 2.5 is often conservatively used for stability and bearing resistance calculations' (p. 5-32); for rammed aggregate piers 5 to 10 under flexible embankment loading and 10 under rigid footings (p. 5-43); 'stress concentration ratios range from 4 to 45 for rigid footings' (p. 5-45).
settlement_methodstroptionalHow the settlement over the columns is worked out. 'stress_ratio' (default): SRF = 1/[1 + as*(n-1)] from n. The others give the settlement ratio (settlement without columns / with them; GEC-13 p. 5-36 prints it as 'n', which is not the stress ratio n) by E_c/E_s off GEC-13 Fig. 5-21, and need E_column and E_soil: 'weighted_modulus' (curve 2, settlement ratio = 1 + as*(E_c/E_s - 1), any E_c/E_s); 'balaam_rigid' (curves 5b, 5c: E_c/E_s 5 to 10, A/A_c 1.75 to 9); 'balaam_flexible' (curve 5a: E_c/E_s = 10, A/A_c 1.5 to 8.5). GEC-13 p. 5-37: the FHWA (1983) Equilibrium Method, 'roughly equivalent to the Balaam relationships', 'represents an average or lower bound estimate suitable for preliminary analyses'; the Priebe curve (priebe_improvement_factor) 'the upper bound effectiveness'. allowed: stress_ratio, weighted_modulus, balaam_rigid, balaam_flexible
E_columnfloatoptionalAggregate column modulus E_c (kPa), with E_soil, for the settlement_method 'weighted_modulus', 'balaam_rigid' or 'balaam_flexible' (E_c/E_s, GEC-13 Fig. 5-21). Refused with 'stress_ratio', which takes n instead. Alias: column_modulus.
q_unreinforcedfloatoptionalUnreinforced bearing capacity (kPa). 0 = not computed.
S_unreinforcedfloatoptionalUnreinforced settlement (mm). 0 = not computed.
Worked example

Ask → 0.76 m aggregate piers on a 1.5 m triangular grid under soft ground — what settlement reduction and bearing improvement do they buy?

call_agent(

    method='aggregate_piers',
    parameters={
        "column_diameter": 0.76,
        "spacing": 1.5,
        "pattern": "triangular",
        "E_soil": 8000.0,
        "S_unreinforced": 100.0,
        "q_unreinforced": 150.0
    },
)

Applicability limits & conventions
  • Aggregate-pier settlement uses the equal-strain settlement-reduction model, not the GEC-13 stiffness-modulus (kg) two-layer method (V-018); the Priebe curve is GEC-13's, drawn for φ = 37.5° only and read at A/Ac 1.6 to 8, and depends on the area-ratio convention supplied (V-019).

4.4 Slope stability & continuum FEM

Will the slope stand? Limit-equilibrium factors of safety and a full 2D finite-element stress/deformation and strength-reduction engine.

4.4.1 slope_stability — Slope stability

Problems it solves

Will the slope stand? The factor of safety of an earth or rock slope against sliding — for a specified surface or the critical one found by search — under drained or undrained conditions, groundwater, surcharge, seismicity, reinforcement, and rapid drawdown, and its probabilistic FOS.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Methods of slices: Ordinary/Fellenius, Bishop simplified (1955), Janbu (corrected), Spencer (1967), Morgenstern–Price, and the rigorous GLE (Fredlund–Krahn) with interslice-force functions.
  • Critical-surface search: circular centre-grid with the best centres refined, entry–exit arcs, random noncircular polylines with differential-evolution / PSO refinement, and weak-layer search; then small circles through each face’s toe and, wherever c′ = 0 soil forms a face, shallow planar surfaces parallel to it. Every trial surface carries the reinforcement it crosses; the result names the governing surface, each family’s minimum and the reinforcement crossing it, and warns when the governing circle ends at a profile end (the profile is then carried on level and the lower FOS reported).
  • Advanced per-layer strength models (the layer strength_model selector): Mohr–Coulomb (default), SHANSEP undrained-strength-ratio (su = S·OCRm·σ′v, with a su,min floor), and Generalized Hoek–Brown for rock (σci, GSI, mi, D).
  • Reinforcement crossing the slip surface: soil nails (pullout + bar-tension capacity, FHWA GEC-7), tieback anchors (allowable tension when the bond zone crosses the surface), horizontal geosynthetic layers, and Ito & Matsui (1975) stabilizing piles, applied in every method as Wright & Duncan (1991) apply them: active (the default; the support reduces the driving force) or passive (the support is added to the resisting force and so divided by F); plus ponded water, tension cracks, and pseudo-static kh.
  • Seismic displacement (Newmark sliding block + Jibson 2007 regression), rapid drawdown (USACE 2-stage / Duncan–Wright–Wong 3-stage), infinite-slope FOS, and probabilistic FOS (FOSM and Monte Carlo).
  • References: Fredlund & Krahn (1977); Bishop (1955); Spencer (1967); Janbu; Duncan, Wright & Brandon (2014); Ito & Matsui (1975); Jibson (2007); validated vs Fredlund–Krahn / ACADS / Duncan / Slide2 (VALIDATION.md, V-015/V-026…V-040).
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Slope Stability
MethodWhat it doesParams
analyze_slopeAnalyze ONE specified slip surface (Fellenius/Bishop/Janbu+f0/Spencer/Morgenstern-Price/GLE). Requires a trial circle (xc/yc/radius) or slip_points. If you do NOT already have a specific trial surface, use search_critical_surface instead — it auto-finds the critical surface and avoids 'circle does not intersect the ground surface' errors. Supports reinforcement (nails/anchors/geosynthetics), ponded water (auto), SHANSEP and Hoek-Brown layer strengths, pseudo-static kh, tension cracks.29
compare_methods_tableRun ALL limit-equilibrium methods (OMS, Bishop, Janbu uncorr/corr, Spencer, Morgenstern-Price) on ONE slip surface and return a side-by-side FOS table (Fredlund & Krahn 1977 style method comparison).26
infinite_slope_fosInfinite-slope (planar translational) factor of safety in closed form (Duncan-Wright): FOS = [c' + (gamma*z*cos^2(beta) - u)*tan(phi')] / (gamma*z*sin(beta)cos(beta)). For the shallow surface-parallel failure mechanism; the depth cancels for cohesionless soil (FOS = tan(phi')/tan(beta) dry, or gamma'/gamma that for seepage at the surface). Use analyze_slope/search_critical_surface for circular/noncircular mechanisms.9
rapid_drawdown_fosRapid-drawdown FOS on a SPECIFIED slip surface: USACE/Army-Corps 2-stage, Lowe-Karafiath 2-stage, or Duncan-Wright-Wong 3-stage. Low-permeability layers respond undrained after fast reservoir drawdown; give them the total-stress R-envelope (soil_layers[].R_c, R_phi) alongside c_prime/phi (R_phi=null => free-draining). Stage 1 = full-pool effective stresses; stage 2 = undrained strength from the R and effective envelopes (Kc-interpolated for Lowe-Karafiath and 3-stage); stage 3 (3-stage only) substitutes the drained strength where lower; final FOS is solved at the drawn-down pool.31
search_rapid_drawdownSEARCH for the critical (minimum-FOS) slip surface under RAPID-DRAWDOWN strengths (Corps 2-stage / Lowe-Karafiath 2-stage / Duncan-Wright-Wong 3-stage). Like search_critical_surface but the per-trial FOS is the rapid-drawdown solve; supports circular and noncircular searches. Use this (not rapid_drawdown_fos) when you do NOT already have a specific trial surface. Low-permeability layers need the R-envelope (soil_layers[].R_c, R_phi).38
yield_accelerationYield (critical) seismic coefficient ky for a SPECIFIED slip surface: the horizontal pseudo-static coefficient kh at which the factor of safety = 1.0 (Newmark critical acceleration, ay = ky*g). Found by bisection on the module's pseudo-static FOS. Feed ky into newmark_displacement or newmark_jibson2007. Provide the surface as xc/yc/radius or slip_points.27
newmark_displacementNewmark rigid-block permanent DOWNSLOPE displacement by double integration of an earthquake acceleration time history against the yield coefficient ky (no upslope rebound). polarity='downslope' (default) is the standard Newmark/Jibson single-block convention (only the destabilizing polarity drives the block); 'rectified' uses the absolute record so both polarities drive it (conservative, ~2x for a symmetric record). Get ky from yield_acceleration. For a quick estimate without a record, use newmark_jibson2007.5
newmark_jibson2007Jibson (2007) regression estimate of Newmark displacement from the critical-acceleration ratio ky/amax (Eq. 6): log10 D[cm] = 0.215 + log10[(1-ky/amax)^2.341 (ky/amax)^-1.438], sigma=0.51 log10. Needs no time history; requires 0 < ky < amax.2
bray_travasarou_2007Bray & Travasarou (2007) simplified seismic DEVIATORIC slope displacement — a fully-coupled stick-slip sliding-block regression that captures sliding-mass flexibility (via the fundamental period Ts) and spectral demand at 1.5*Ts, which the rigid-block Jibson/integration models don't. Returns P(D=0) (prob. of negligible <=1 cm displacement) and the median non-zero displacement (16/84% via sigma_ln=0.66). A period-dependent cross-check for Jibson.5
search_critical_surfaceSearch for the critical slip surface (minimum FOS): circular centre-grid, entry-exit arcs, random noncircular polylines, differential-evolution noncircular refinement, PSO, or weak-layer-biased search.35
fosm_fosFOSM / Taylor-series reliability of the FOS on a fixed slip surface (Duncan 2000): central finite differences at +/- 1 sigma per variable -> COV_F, beta (normal + lognormal), probability of failure, per-variable variance contributions. Supports both independent per-layer scalar variables AND a correlated depth-varying su-gradient law (see 'variables').28
monte_carlo_fosMonte Carlo FOS distribution on a fixed slip surface (optionally re-searching the critical surface per realization): samples layer parameters (normal/lognormal), returns pf, FOS statistics and histogram.32
Parameters of search_critical_surface
ParameterTypeDescription
surface_pointsarrayrequiredGround surface as [[x,y], ...] array (x increasing).
soil_layersarrayrequiredArray of soil-layer dicts: {top_elevation, bottom_elevation, gamma (all required); name, gamma_sat, phi, c_prime, cu, analysis_mode ('drained'|'undrained'), ru, bottom_boundary_points optional}. Per-layer strength_model: 'mohr_coulomb' (default), 'shansep' (su = shansep_S ocr^shansep_m sigma'_v; fields shansep_S, shansep_m, ocr, su_min) 'hoek_brown' (Generalized Hoek-Brown; fields hb_sigci kPa, hb_gsi, hb_mi, hb_D) or 'anisotropic' (undrained su varies with the slice-base inclination alpha; fields su_active [kPa, ACTIVE/crest zone, alpha>=+45deg], su_dss [direct simple shear, alpha=0], su_passive [PASSIVE/toe zone, alpha<=-45deg] — su_active>=su_dss>=su_passive for K>1 clays; Casagrande-Carrillo sin(2alpha) interpolation; standard toe-at-low-x slope). For rapid_drawdown_fos, low-permeability layers also take the total-stress R-envelope R_c (kPa) and R_phi (deg); R_phi omitted/null => free-draining.
gwt_pointsarrayoptionalGroundwater table [[x,y],...]. If above the ground surface, ponded water is auto-detected (water weight + horizontal hydrostatic thrust applied as external loads).
khfloatoptionalHorizontal pseudo-static seismic coefficient (acts on soil weight only).
surchargefloatoptionalVertical surcharge (kPa). A single loaded zone; use 'surcharges' for several distinct loaded areas.
surcharge_x_rangearrayoptional[x_start, x_end] extent of the single 'surcharge'.
surchargesarrayoptionalSeveral distinct surcharge zones (bench + crest loads, etc.): [{pressure kPa, x_start, x_end}, ...]. Each zone's pressure is summed at any x it covers, ON TOP OF the single 'surcharge'/'surcharge_x_range'. Represent a linearly-varying (trapezoidal) load as its mean uniform pressure or as several thin zones.
tension_crack_depthfloatoptionalTension crack depth at the crest (m).
tension_crack_water_depthfloatoptionalWater depth in the tension crack (m).
tension_crack_sidestroptionalWhich crest end the tension crack is on: 'entry' (default, low-x / slip-surface entry) or 'exit' (high-x). Put it on whichever side the crest is on; no need to mirror the slope. allowed: entry, exit
tension_crack_modelstroptionalTension-crack mechanism: 'strength' (default) keeps the cracked wedge as zero-shear-strength driving soil; 'truncation' removes it from the sliding mass (mass ends at the vertical crack face, as Slide2/UTEXAS do). Truncation is less conservative. allowed: strength, truncation
reverse_curvaturestroptionalA circle whose centre is below the ground where it comes out would turn back above its centre (Slide2: reverse curvature). 'tension_crack' (default, as Slide2) closes it with a dry vertical crack; 'discard' drops such circles from searches. allowed: tension_crack, discard
pore_pressure_pointsarrayoptionalDiscrete pore-pressure field as [[x, z, u], ...] triples (u in kPa) -- a flow-net / TIN sampling. When given, the base pore pressure at each slice is interpolated from this field (linear on the Delaunay triangulation, nearest-node fallback outside the hull, suction clamped to 0), OVERRIDING the gwt_points piezometric line and per-layer ru. The ponded-water buttress still comes from gwt_points, so set BOTH for a reservoir over a flow-net field.
nailsarrayoptionalSoil nails (per metre of slope run): [{x_head, z_head, length required; inclination deg below horizontal=15, bar_diameter mm=25, drill_hole_diameter mm=150, fy MPa=420, bond_stress kPa=100, spacing_h m=1.5, support_convention}]. Capacity = min(pullout behind slip surface, bar tensile)/spacing_h (FHWA GEC-7).
anchorsarrayoptionalTieback anchors: [{x_head, z_head, length, T_allow kN/m required; inclination=15, support_convention}]. Full T_allow applied when the bond zone crosses the slip surface.
geosyntheticsarrayoptionalHorizontal geosynthetic layers: [{elevation, T_allow kN/m required; x_start, x_end, support_convention optional}]. Every support (nails, anchors, geosynthetics, piles) acts at the base of the slice it crosses (Wright & Duncan 1991). support_convention: 'active' (default; Duncan & Wright Method A / Slide2 Active: the force is not divided by F and reduces the driving side -- give the ALLOWABLE force) or 'passive' (Method B / Slide2 Passive: divided by F with the soil strength -- give the ULTIMATE force; lower FOS for the same force). All methods.
stabilizing_pilesarrayoptionalSingle-row stabilizing/micro piles crossing the slope (Ito & Matsui 1975 or a specified shear): [{x required; spacing m=1.0 (D1); z_head, z_toe optional}]. Set the resistance EITHER by shear_capacity (kN per pile; per-metre force = shear_capacity/spacing) OR ito_matsui=true with diameter (m; D2=spacing-diameter) and optional c/phi/gamma (default: soil layer) giving the Ito-Matsui plastic lateral force integrated from head to slip surface. force_direction 'horizontal' (default) or 'normal'. support_convention 'active' (default) or 'passive' as for geosynthetics. Stabilizing force at the slip crossing.
reinforcement_forcefloatoptionalSingle equivalent horizontal reinforcement force (kN/m). Simpler alternative to nails/anchors.
reinforcement_elevationfloatoptionalElevation of the equivalent reinforcement force (m).
surface_typestroptionalSearch strategy. 'entry_exit' grids circular arcs between entry/exit windows; 'noncircular_de' refines random polylines with scipy differential evolution. allowed: circular, entry_exit, noncircular, noncircular_de, pso, weak_layer
methodstroptionalLimit-equilibrium method (noncircular searches use spencer when 'bishop' is requested). Cost per trial surface, measured on four pinned slopes: fellenius about the same as bishop, janbu about twice bishop, and spencer, morgenstern_price and gle each about 30 to 40 times bishop at 30 slices and 40 to 70 times at 60 slices. A whole search costs less than that ratio where it scans with Bishop (the centre grid's refinement, the toe circles): the default 10 x 10 centre grid took 2-3 s with bishop and 14-16 s with spencer, a 10 x 10 or 12 x 12 entry_exit grid 2 s and 60-70 s, a 30 x 30 entry_exit grid at 60 slices 21 s and 972 s; the noncircular searches, scored with Spencer at their defaults (500 trials, 5 points), took 6-7 s (noncircular), 3-7 s (weak_layer) and 10-12 s (noncircular_de), 41 s where differential evolution scored 2,325 surfaces (development laptop; the app's host up to twice as long). On the circles of these slopes bishop and spencer gave FOS within 0.3 % of each other. Which method to use is the engineer's call; bishop_screen keeps the method and scans with Bishop. allowed: fellenius, bishop, janbu, spencer, morgenstern_price, gle
x_rangearrayoptional[xmin, xmax] for circle center search.
y_rangearrayoptional[ymin, ymax] for circle center search.
x_entry_rangearrayoptional[xmin, xmax] window for the slip surface's ENTRY: its low-x end, whichever way the slope faces (the toe side of a slope rising to the right, the crest side of one falling to the right).
x_exit_rangearrayoptional[xmin, xmax] window for the slip surface's EXIT: its high-x end. Windows given the other way round (entry wholly right of exit) are swapped, and the result's warnings say so.
nxintoptionalGrid divisions in x (or entry divisions for entry_exit).
nyintoptionalGrid divisions in y (or exit divisions for entry_exit).
n_trialsintoptionalRandom trials for noncircular searches.
n_pointsintoptionalPolyline vertices for noncircular searches.
n_slicesintoptionalNumber of slices per trial.
seedintoptionalRandom seed for reproducible noncircular/PSO/DE searches.
time_budget_sfloatoptionalTime budget of the whole search in seconds (at most 600). The main search scores its centres or entry/exit pairs coarse first and stops at 80 % of the budget; the result is then the lowest surface found, and warnings and search_ranges.time_budget say what was scored of how many, at what spacing, the run time projected for the whole search, and what was not run. Raise it for a long search you mean to wait for.
bishop_screenbooloptionalcircular and entry_exit searches with spencer / morgenstern_price / gle: score every centre or pair with Bishop's simplified method, then re-score the lowest (at least 10, every one within 5 % of the lowest, at most 30) with the method itself; the reported FOS is the method's own. On four pinned slopes it found the same surfaces and FOS as the unscreened search in 35-60 % of the time on the default centre grid, 15-30 % on 10 x 10 and 12 x 12 entry_exit grids and 3 % on a 30 x 30 entry_exit grid at 60 slices (33 s against 972 s). Not applied where supports are modelled; noncircular searches are not screened.
m_alpha_rulestroptionalWhich slices the m_alpha < 0.2 check looks at (every search leaves out a surface that fails it, as Slide2 does with its 'Check malpha < 0.2' setting on). 'frictional': slices with phi' > 0; on a phi' = 0 slice m_alpha = cos(a) does not change the FOS, so leaving such a surface out only raises the minimum. 'every_slice': every slice, as Slide2 checks. allowed: frictional, every_slice
tolfloatoptionalConvergence tolerance for the iterative methods.

                ],

                        10,
                        0
                ],
                [
                        25,
                        10
                ],
                [
                        45,
                        10
                ]
        ],
        "soil_layers": [
                {
                        "name": "clayey sand",
                        "top_elevation": 10.0,
                        "bottom_elevation": -10.0,
                        "gamma": 19.0,
                        "phi": 28.0,
                        "c_prime": 12.0,
                        "analysis_mode": "drained"
                }
        ],
        "surface_type": "entry_exit",
        "method": "bishop",
        "x_entry_range": [
                10,
                20
        ],
        "x_exit_range": [

1,418 trial surfaces were evaluated in the entry–exit search; the minimum governs.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • Pore pressure is a piezometric surface or per-layer ru, not an arbitrary interpolated flow-net grid (V-029).
  • The tension crack is entry-side and keeps the cracked wedge as zero-strength driving soil with full hydrostatic thrust — a conservative convention vs mass-truncation codes (V-026).
  • When a rigorous method finds no solution on a surface that supports cross, the result gives no FOS for that method and says so, rather than an unreinforced value.

4.4.2 fem2d — 2D finite-element analysis (fem2d)

Problems it solves

When limit equilibrium is not enough: a full 2D plane-strain finite-element engine for stress and deformation of soil masses, slope stability by strength reduction, bearing collapse, excavation unloading, seepage, and coupled consolidation — with structural beam members for walls.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Elements: T6 quadratic triangle (default, collapse-accurate), CST, Q4, and 2-node Euler–Bernoulli beams.
  • Constitutive models: linear elastic, Mohr–Coulomb (3D-principal return mapping, non-associated flow), and Hardening Soil (Schanz, Vermeer & Bonnier 1999).
  • Strength-reduction method for slope FOS (Griffiths & Lane 1999), within 2 % across meshes once four or more elements span the slope; staged construction, with movements reported per stage and counted from the end of the in-situ stage; initial-stress relaxation for tunnels/cavities.
  • Staged excavation (analyze_excavation): half of a symmetric excavation, in-situ stresses by K0, then one stage per lift that removes the soil and releases the forces it carried; the wall is wished in place and each strut installed stress-free when the dig reaches it. Below the water table the excavation is dewatered by default, with steady seepage under the wall (excavation_water: 'dewatered', or 'full' / 'level'); the result gives each stage, the wall’s largest moment and shear with their depths, the net water pressure and the upward gradient in front of the wall. Benchmarked against the USS Steel Sheet Piling Design Manual’s cantilever in granular soil (Mmax within 3 %).
  • Steady/transient seepage and Biot consolidation (staggered, and a monolithic Taylor–Hood u–p scheme); PLAXIS-style calc-package plots.
  • References: Griffiths & Lane (1999); de Souza Neto et al. (2008); Clausen et al. (2006); Schanz et al. (1999); validated vs Griffiths–Lane, the Prandtl solution (~2%), and Itasca FLAC (VALIDATION.md, V-023/V-024).
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
FEM 2D
MethodWhat it doesParams
fem2d_hs_parametersEstimate HS/HSsmall model parameters for sand from relative density (Brinkgreve et al. 2010).1
fem2d_gravityElastic gravity analysis of a rectangular soil column (plane strain FEM).8
fem2d_foundationElastic strip foundation analysis on a half-space (plane strain FEM).9
fem2d_footing_capacityUltimate bearing capacity of a rigid strip footing by FEM load-control to collapse (plane-strain, the FE analogue of a bearing-capacity calc). Validated vs Prandtl Nc=5.14. Use element_type='t6' (CST locks and never collapses).18
fem2d_slope_srmSlope stability FOS via Strength Reduction Method (plane strain FEM).20

fem2d_local_fosLocal (pointwise) factor-of-safety map for a slope: runs the SRM then evaluates local_FOS = Mohr-Coulomb available shear / mobilized shear at each element using the ORIGINAL strengths. At the critical SRF the minimum local FOS ~ the global SRM FOS and the low-FOS band is the failure mass. Returns summary stats (the full field is for plotting).20
fem2d_excavationStaged excavation in front of an embedded wall (plane strain FEM): in-situ K0 stresses, then lifts with struts installed as the excavation reaches them; half of a symmetric excavation.23
fem2d_seepageSteady-state seepage analysis (Laplace equation, CST elements).6
fem2d_consolidationCoupled Biot consolidation analysis (settlement + pore pressure dissipation).17
fem2d_stagedStaged construction analysis (multi-phase, activate/deactivate soil groups and beams); reports each stage's own movement, the cumulative movement and the movement since a reference stage.12

ParameterTypeDescription

depthfloatoptionalDepth below lowest surface (m). Default the larger of 2*H and 10 m.
nxintoptionalMesh divisions in x.
nyintoptionalMesh divisions in y.

srf_rangearrayoptional[min, max] SRF search range.

n_load_stepsintoptionalNumber of load increments applied before the analysis / SRF sweep.

The SRF at which the Newton solve stops converging is the FEM factor of safety; T6 quadratic elements are used by default.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • CST elements lock in plastic collapse (Prandtl Nc overshoots) — use T6 for collapse/FOS work; CST is for elastic/seepage/Biot only.
  • It is a research-grade solver, not a substitute for a commercial FE package under QA; a far-field boundary must be placed far enough to avoid truncation error. The strength reduction warns when the mesh has too few elements across the slope, and when φ = 0 soil lies below the toe with level ground shorter than 1.5 times its depth (a deep circle cannot form). By default over such soil the model carries the level ground to twice that depth each side, so Taylor’s deep circle can form (a slightly higher FOS than before and about twice the run time for those runs); x_extend sets the margins, one number or a (left, right) pair. An undrained layer with Poisson’s ratio below 0.45 is warned: use 0.49.

4.5 Seismic & liquefaction

Site response, seismic earth pressures, liquefaction triggering, and ground-motion processing.

4.5.1 seismic_geotech — Seismic geotechnics

Problems it solves

Site seismic geotechnics: the ASCE-7 site class and design coefficients, Mononobe–Okabe seismic earth pressures on walls, SPT liquefaction triggering, and post-liquefaction residual strength.

Methods & theories implemented
  • ASCE 7 site classification from Vs30, N-bar, or su-bar, with Fpga/Fa/Fv and design spectral values.
  • Mononobe–Okabe active/passive seismic earth-pressure coefficients (KAE/KPE), battered-wall correct, with the seismic thrust and point of application.
  • SPT liquefaction triggering (NCEER / Youd et al. 2001 simplified procedure) and residual strength.
  • References: ASCE 7; Mononobe–Okabe; NCEER (1997) / Youd et al. (2001); validated vs GEC-11 Ex E7 (V-011, KAE within 0.06%).

4.5.2 liquefaction — Liquefaction (unified tool)

Problems it solves

The single, discoverable liquefaction-triggering tool: is the ground liquefiable, and what is the factor of safety by depth — from SPT or CPT data, by the method your work requires.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Auto-routes by input type and method: CPT (qc/fs) → Boulanger & Idriss (2014) via liquepy, with LPI / LSN / LDI indices.
  • SPT (N160) → Boulanger & Idriss (2014) by default, or NCEER / Youd et al. (2001) via method='nceer2001' for code-compliance work.
  • References: Boulanger & Idriss (2014); NCEER (1997) / Youd et al. (2001).
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Liquefaction

  • Routing lives at the agent layer (no cross-module import); the underlying per-module functions (liquepy, seismic_geotech) remain directly callable.

4.5.3 liquepy — Liquefaction building blocks (liquepy)

Problems it solves

Direct access to the Boulanger & Idriss (2014) liquefaction building blocks and field correlations, wrapping the liquepy library — for when you want the individual CRR/CSR/MSF/Kσ terms rather than the unified tool.

Methods & theories implemented
  • B&I-2014 CPT triggering (packaged run_bi2014) with LPI/LSN/LDI.
  • B&I-2014 SPT triggering composed from the module-level building blocks (CRRM7.5, rd, CSR, Kσ) plus the SPT fines correction and MSF.
  • Field correlations (Vs, Dr, G0 from N).
  • References: Boulanger & Idriss (2014); the liquepy library. Requires the [liquepy] extra.

Nonlinear finite-element site response and element-test simulation, wrapping OpenSeesPy: cyclic direct-simple-shear behaviour of liquefiable sand and one-dimensional ground response.

Methods & theories implemented

  • One-dimensional nonlinear site response (soil column, base motion), run in a separate process with a time limit (time_limit_s, default 600 s).

Site response is checked against the OpenSees wiki’s layered soil column (total stress, McGann & Arduino) and the OpenSeesPy effective-stress example, Kramer (1996) §7.2’s uniform damped layer on elastic rock, and pyStrata. One-dimensional equivalent-linear site response (a SHAKE-type analysis): amplification of a base motion through a layered soil column to a surface spectrum and profiles of peak strain and acceleration.

Methods & theories implemented

4.5.6 seismic_signals — Ground-motion signal processing

Problems it solves

Ground-motion signal processing: response spectra, intensity measures, and rotated components from an acceleration record — the quantities behind a seismic demand.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Response spectra by Nigam and Jennings (1969), in sub-steps at short periods (the OpenSees site response's code); Fourier processing (eqsig); rotated-component spectra RotD0/RotD50/RotD100 (Boore 2010) from the same time-domain oscillator responses; Arias intensity, significant duration, and other intensity measures.
  • References: Nigam and Jennings (1969); Boore (2010); the eqsig library. Requires the [seismic-signals] extra.
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Seismic Signals
MethodWhat it doesParams
response_spectrumCompute the response spectrum, every period by Nigam and Jennings (1969): the record linear between samples, in sub-steps of at most a twentieth of the period, the peak read between samples (the OpenSees site response uses the same code).6
intensity_measuresCompute earthquake intensity measures (Arias intensity, CAV, significant duration).6
rotd_spectrumCompute rotated spectral acceleration (RotD0/RotD50/RotD100 or any percentile) from two horizontal components (Boore 2010): each component's oscillator response by Nigam and Jennings (1969), the record linear between samples, rotated through 0-179 deg, the peak at each angle read between samples. RotD100 of a component paired with zeros is that component's response_spectrum.8
signal_processingBandpass filtering and/or baseline correction of acceleration time history.6

4.6 Site characterization & geostatistics

Turning borings, cones, and lab data into a modelled ground — parse, visualize, correlate, and interpolate.

4.6.1 subsurface — Subsurface data I/O (DIGGS / GEF / AGS4)

Problems it solves

Getting field and lab data into a modelled ground: parse and validate DIGGS, GEF/BRO-XML CPT, and AGS4 files, visualize parameters against depth, and compute trend statistics — the ingest side of characterization.

Methods & theories implemented
  • DIGGS parser (20 test types) with Plotly parameter-vs-depth, Atterberg, plan-view and trend plots; the plan view labels its axes from the stated coordinate system.
  • DIGGS 2.6 writer (write_diggs) for logs and lab results read off a report: records given inline or as saved JSON files, checked against the schema and read back, with cross-checks (lab links, drives against sample intervals, readings below the hole’s depth) that never change a value; groundwater not encountered is never written as a level, an unknown position is never written as 0, and a printed refusal is kept as one.
  • Folded format adapters: GEF/BRO-XML CPT and borehole parsing (pygef), AGS4 read/validate (python-ags4; an optional extra from the release after 5.33.0), and DIGGS schema/dictionary validation (pydiggs).
  • References: the DIGGS, GEF, and AGS4 standards; pygef / python-ags4 / pydiggs. Requires the [subsurface] extra for the format adapters.

4.6.2 gstools — Geostatistics (kriging, random fields & conditional simulation)

Problems it solves

Geostatistics for spatially variable ground: fit a variogram to scattered data, krige a property between borings, generate correlated random fields for spatial-variability studies, and find the probability that a TOTAL over a footprint exceeds a value — the volume of rock above an excavation level, the area where soft soil runs below a level — by conditional simulation.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Variogram estimation and model fitting; ordinary/simple/universal kriging (the smoothed best estimate between points, with the kriged surface’s totals over plan polygons and Gaussian pointwise expectations; a large grid goes to a CSV); unconditional random-field generation, wrapping GSTools.
  • Conditional simulation: many realizations that honour the observations, by conditioning by kriging (Journel & Huijbregts 1978; Chilès & Delfiner 2012 §7.3.1), each integrated over plan polygons and levels on the same realizations: mean, percentiles, the chance of any encounter, an exceedance table with standard errors, a convergence table, CSV files, an exceedance curve and a plan map of P(z > level). GSTools’ CondSRF is offered to reproduce a CondSRF notebook; it spreads totals too widely, so it is not the default.
  • References: the GSTools library (Müller et al.). Installed with the app (no extra needed).
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Geostatistics
MethodWhat it doesParams
krigingKriging (ordinary/simple/universal): ONE smoothed best estimate of a property between points -- the mean surface and its kriging variance. It understates the spread and cannot give the probability of a total over an area (use conditional_simulation).28
variogramEstimate and fit an empirical variogram from spatial data (sill, range, nugget).6
random_fieldGenerate ONE UNconditioned 2D random field (mean + correlated variation). It does NOT honour any data; for realizations that pass through observations use conditional_simulation.12
conditional_simulationRealizations that honour the data (conditioned random field), each integrated over plan polygons: probabilities of a TOTAL over an area -- volume above/below a level (rock to excavate, fill), area, any encounter -- with percentiles, exceedance, CSV files and figures.30
Parameters of kriging
ParameterTypeDescription
xarrayrequiredX-coordinates of measurement points (m).
yarrayrequiredY-coordinates of measurement points (m).
valuesarrayrequiredMeasured values at each point.
model_typestroptionalGSTools covariance model. allowed: Gaussian, Exponential, Matern, Spherical, Linear, Stable, Rational, Cubic, HyperSpherical
kriging_typestroptionalordinary = unknown constant mean; simple = known mean (the sample mean of these observations); universal = linear drift in x and y. allowed: ordinary, simple, universal
grid_x_minfloatoptionalGrid X minimum (m). Omitted: the data's x range less 10%.
grid_x_maxfloatoptionalGrid X maximum (m). Omitted: the data's x range plus 10%.
grid_y_minfloatoptionalGrid Y minimum (m). Omitted: from the data, as x.
grid_y_maxfloatoptionalGrid Y maximum (m). Omitted: from the data, as x.

n_grid_yintoptionalGrid points in Y.

len_scalefloatoptionalCorrelation length (m). Omitted: a third of the data extent. With fit_variogram=true it is only the starting guess and is overridden by the fit.
nuggetfloatoptionalNugget variance (measurement error + variation below the data spacing); with a nugget the surface does not pass exactly through the data. With fit_variogram=true the nugget is fitted too, unless fit_nugget=false.
fit_variogrambooloptionalFit variance, len_scale AND nugget to the empirical variogram, overriding values given for them (the fitted values are returned). Refused with too few lag classes: then set false and give variance and len_scale.
fit_nuggetbooloptionalWith fit_variogram: false holds the nugget at the value given (e.g. from the measurement error or twinned borings) and fits only variance and len_scale. Without fit_variogram nothing is fitted and true is refused.
regionsarrayoptionalPlan regions: [{name, polygon: [[x, y], ...], level}], level one number or a list of levels to sweep (same units as values, e.g. an elevation in m). Totals over the cells whose centre is inside the polygon (concave shapes fine): volume_above = sum(max(z - level, 0) x cell area), area_above = cell area where z > level (the 'below' versions mirror it). Here from the kriging only: the kriged surface's totals, and Gaussian POINTWISE expectations (expected volume, expected area, mean cell probability). These are expectations cell by cell; the probability that a TOTAL exceeds a value needs conditional_simulation.
cell_sizefloatoptionalCell size (m) for the region totals; default the smallest round size giving at most ~3,000 cells.

marginfloatoptionalMargin (m) of the region lattice around the regions.

figuresbooloptionalDraw the kriging map: a plan, to scale, of the kriged mean and the kriging standard deviation as labelled contours, the standard deviation with a colour scale too (PNG + interactive). Set false in a sweep of many calls.
namesarrayoptionalObservation names (e.g. boring IDs), one per point; label the map.
value_namestroptionalWhat the values are, in the logs' words (e.g. 'top of hard rock elevation'); names the map. Give it.
value_unitstroptionalUnit of the values (e.g. 'm').

A list of {name, polygon: [[x, y], ...]} (closed, 3 points or more) or {name, line: [[x, y], ...]} (open, 2 or more), in the same x, y as the observations, with kind 'property_line' (drawn dash-dot) or 'outline' (default). Drawing only: they change no number.
observations_namestroptionalWhat the observation points are, in the logs' words (e.g. 'Borings', 'CPT soundings'): the map legend's name for them. 'Observations' when not given.
Applicability limits & conventions
  • The spread is what the chosen model implies: a Gaussian, stationary field with the covariance model, variance and length scale given (or computed from the data and echoed). With few borings these cannot be checked against the data and usually move the answer more than the method does — run cases.
  • Plan view (2D) only; inequality data (a boring that ended above rock) by rejection sampling.

4.7 Reliability & sensitivity

The variability engine: propagate parameter uncertainty to a reliability index and a probability of failure, and find which input governs.

4.7.1 reliability — Reliability engine

Problems it solves

The variability engine: turn any deterministic method into a probabilistic one and report the reliability index β and probability of failure Pf — because with soil COVs of 10–40% the honest deliverable is a distribution, not a lone factor of safety.

Methods & theories implemented
  • FOSM (First-Order Second-Moment), PEM (Rosenblueth point-estimate), Monte Carlo (with Cholesky correlation and Latin Hypercube), and native FORM (Hasofer–Lind design point).
  • A published COV knowledge base (Duncan 2000; TC304; Phoon & Kulhawy) queried by cov_guidance; Vanmarcke spatial-averaging variance reduction; combined COV.
  • Ready-made wrappers: bearing_capacity_reliability, axial_pile_reliability, slope_reliability.
  • References: Duncan (2000); Phoon & Kulhawy (1999); Baecher & Christian; Vanmarcke (1977); validated vs Duncan (2000) reliability example.
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Property Variability
MethodWhat it doesParams
cov_guidancePublished COV ranges for soil/rock properties with full provenance: Duncan (2000) Table 1, ISSMGE-TC304 (2021) site-specific statistics (clay/sand/rock), Phoon & Kulhawy (1999) transformation uncertainty (via UFC 3-220-20). Use to pick a defensible cov for the engines.4
combined_covCombine inherent + measurement + transformation COVs (UFC 3-220-20 Eq. 7-5), optionally with Vanmarcke spatial-averaging variance reduction on the inherent part. All COVs as fractions (0.3 = 30%).4
variance_reductionVanmarcke variance reduction Gamma^2(L/delta) for spatial averaging over a failure surface/pile length. Give delta directly or a soil_type to use published scale-of-fluctuation guidance (Cami et al. 2020 / ISSMGE-TC304 2021).4
Reliability
MethodWhat it doesParams
fosmFOSM / Taylor-series reliability (Duncan 2000, UFC 3-220-20): central differences at +/-1 sigma -> moments of g, beta (normal+lognormal), pf, and the per-variable variance-contribution table (which variable matters). 2n+1 g-evaluations; supports correlation.4
pemRosenblueth point-estimate method (UFC 3-220-20 Eqs. 7-13/7-14): 2^n evaluations at mu+/-sigma (correlation-adjusted weights), or the 2n+1 'multiplicative' reduced scheme for many variables.5
monte_carloMonte Carlo simulation: seeded numpy sampling (optional Latin Hypercube), correlation via Cholesky in normal space, empirical pf with 95% CI + convergence trace, histogram, lognormal-fit beta. Its variables are scalars; for a property that varies across a site and must honour borings (e.g. a rock surface under a footprint), use gstools.conditional_simulation.8
formNative FORM (Hasofer-Lind / Rackwitz-Fiessler): HL-RF iteration with equivalent-normal transformation of non-normal variables; exact for the linear/lognormal cases. Returns beta, pf, design point x*, and alpha sensitivity vector (alpha^2 = uncertainty share).5
Parameters of monte_carlo
ParameterTypeDescription
variablesobjectrequiredRandom variables: {name: {mean, cov or std, dist, lower, upper}}. dist one of ['normal', 'lognormal', 'uniform', 'triangular'] (default normal). lower/upper truncate normal/lognormal or bound uniform/triangular. Example: {'su': {'mean': 50, 'cov': 0.3, 'dist': 'lognormal'}}.
g_expressionstrrequiredPerformance function of the variable names. With convention='fos' write a FACTOR OF SAFETY (failure at g<1), e.g. 'R/S'; with 'margin' a margin (failure at g<0), e.g. 'R - S'. Math functions allowed (sqrt, log, exp, tan, radians, ...).
conventionstroptional'fos': g is a factor of safety (failure g<1, lognormal beta reported). 'margin': g = R-S (failure g<0). allowed: fos, margin
correlationobjectoptionalPairwise correlations {'a,b': rho} or full matrix [[...]] in variable order. Omit for independent variables.
nintoptionalRealizations. Aim n >= 10/pf.
seedintoptionalRNG seed for reproducibility.
samplingstroptional'lhs' = Latin Hypercube (variance reduction). allowed: random, lhs
n_binsintoptionalHistogram bins.
Worked example

Ask → Resistance R (mean 500, COV 20%, lognormal) against load S (mean 300, COV 15%) — 50,000 Monte-Carlo trials: what is the reliability index and the probability of failure?

call_agent(
    agent_name='reliability',
    method='monte_carlo',
    parameters={
        "variables": {
                "R": {
                        "mean": 500.0,
                        "cov": 0.2,
                        "dist": "lognormal"
                },
                "S": {
                        "mean": 300.0,
                        "cov": 0.15,
                        "dist": "normal"
                }
        },
        "g_expression": "R - S",
        "convention": "margin",
        "n": 50000,
        "seed": 42
    },
)

This is the payoff of the whole architecture: any deterministic method plugs into the same g() contract and returns β and Pf instead of a lone number.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • The performance function is a scalar g(values); correlated depth-varying strength laws with a single gradient variable are a documented scope edge (V-030).

4.7.2 salib — Global sensitivity analysis (SALib)

Problems it solves

Which uncertain input actually governs the answer? Global sensitivity analysis apportions the variance of a model output to its inputs, so investigation and design effort go where they matter.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Sobol variance-based indices (first-order and total) and Morris elementary-effects screening, wrapping SALib; sample generation and index computation.
  • References: Sobol; Morris; the SALib library. Requires the [salib] extra.
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Sensitivity Analysis
MethodWhat it doesParams
sobol_analysisONE CALL Sobol variance-based sensitivity: samples, evaluates the model (an expression or a calculation-module spec) at every point, returns S1/ST indices only. Use this, not sobol_sample + sobol_analyze.9
morris_analysisONE CALL Morris elementary-effects screening: samples, evaluates the model (an expression or a calculation-module spec) at every point, returns mu*/sigma only. Cheaper than Sobol: evaluations = n_trajectories*(D+1).9
sobol_sampleGenerate Sobol quasi-random sample matrix for variance-based sensitivity analysis (two-step: YOU evaluate the model on every row, then sobol_analyze). Prefer sobol_analysis, which does it in one call.5

4.7.3 pystra — Structural reliability (pystra)

Problems it solves

Structural reliability for an explicit limit-state function: the reliability index and probability of failure by FORM, SORM, or Monte Carlo, with a full distribution library and correlation.

Methods & theories implemented
  • FORM / SORM / Monte Carlo on a user limit-state function, wrapping pystra (the Python port of FERUM).
  • References: the pystra library. Requires the [pystra] extra.
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Reliability
MethodWhat it doesParams

sorm_analysisSecond Order Reliability Method (SORM) — improved probability with curvature correction.3
monte_carlo_analysisCrude Monte Carlo reliability analysis — estimate failure probability by random sampling.4
Applicability limits & conventions
  • Complements the geotechnical reliability engine; use pystra for a general structural limit state and reliability for the geotechnical wrappers + COV database.

4.8 Structural analysis

Cross-section properties, reinforced-concrete section capacity, and elastic frame / continuous-beam analysis.

4.8.1 section_props — Cross-section properties

Problems it solves

Structural cross-section properties for steel and generic shapes: area, moments of inertia, elastic and plastic moduli, radii of gyration, torsion and warping constants — the inputs every member check starts from. Dimensions in mm.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Exact closed-form integration over the section outline (Green’s theorem): parametric rectangle / circle / CHS / RHS / I-section, plus arbitrary polygon outlines.
  • Torsion and warping constants from the published closed forms — the exact St. Venant series for a rectangle, Bredt for closed boxes, El Darwish & Johnston / AISC for I-sections; arbitrary outlines fall back to a finite-difference Prandtl solve.
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Cross-Section Analysis
MethodWhat it doesParams
section_propertiesProperties of parametric shapes (rectangle/circle/CHS/RHS/I): A, I, Z, S, r, J, warping. Dimensions in mm. One material; a multi-material PILE's composite EI (RC, concrete-filled pipe) is lateral_pile.composite_section_ei.10
polygon_sectionProperties of an arbitrary closed polygon section from vertex coordinates (mm).3
Applicability limits & conventions
  • Geometric properties only — no member design checks; nominal member capacity comes from the design reference layer as it grows.

4.8.2 concrete_props — RC section analysis

Problems it solves

Reinforced-concrete rectangular sections: gross and cracked stiffness, cracking moment, nominal moment capacity (sagging/hogging), and the N-M interaction diagram. mm and MPa in, kN·m out.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Strain-compatibility section analysis against the ACI 318-19 material model (Ec = 4700√f’c, rectangular stress block with ACI β1, fr = 0.62√f’c).
  • Capacities are NOMINAL — apply code φ factors separately.

Elastic frame and continuous-beam analysis: reactions, member moment/shear/axial envelopes, and deflections for 2D/3D skeletal structures. SI units (m, kN, kPa).

4.10 Also available: native soil correlations

SPT field corrections (N → N60 → (N1)60 per Youd et al. 2001 / Liao & Whitman), Bolton stress-dilatancy, the small-strain Gmax family (Vs, CPT, Hardin-Black, Andersen), Ishibashi & Zhang modulus-reduction/damping curves, and Brinkgreve HS-parameter estimation are implemented natively (geotech_common.soil_properties, seismic_geotech.dynamic_properties, fem2d.hs_correlations) and exposed through the subsurface, seismic, and fem2d agents. The former third-party groundhog wrapper was removed in favor of these.

Chapter 5The reference library

The agent doesn’t just compute — it reads the standards back to you. geotech-references is a companion package of digitized design manuals: their tables and equations as callable lookups, their chapter text in a full-text search index, and their figures in a searchable catalog paired with a vision read-off. There are 34 reference modules.

5.2 Find with text, read with pixels

Retrieval is lexical: reference_search runs a full-text (SQLite FTS5) query over the chapter text and equation captions, expanded with a curated synonym map so a query for “passive resistance” also finds “Kp”. That roughly quadrupled recall@5 in the retrieval eval with no disturbance to the top hit. Figures are handled the same way for search, then differently for reading: figure_search finds a chart by meaning, and read_reference_figure renders the actual page and hands it to a vision model to read a value off the axes — because a design chart’s value lives in its pixels, not its caption.

Why not image embeddings?

CLIP-style image embeddings were evaluated and rejected — they are a poor fit for axis-labelled line charts. The architecture is deliberately “find lexically, read visually.” This keeps retrieval cheap and explainable while still getting an accurate value off the chart.

In agent workflows all of this is reached through the consult_references sub-agent described in Chapter 3, so the primary agent stays focused on the analysis while a scoped consultant handles citations and figure read-offs.

Chapter 6Geometry import & model setup

Real analyses start from a real cross-section — a CAD file or a PDF drawing, not a set of hand-typed coordinates. Three modules get geometry in and a fourth gets a calc package out; a fifth orchestrates a staged, human-gated model build.

6.1 DXF import

dxf_import reads a DXF, discovers its layers, and converts polylines into the SlopeGeometry and FEM inputs the analysis modules consume. The workflow is discover → parse → build: list the layers, map them to surface / soil boundaries / water table / reinforcement, then build the model. It needs the [dxf] extra (ezdxf).

6.2 PDF cross-section import

pdf_import extracts geometry from a PDF drawing two ways: vector extraction (PyMuPDF get_drawings() for exact line work) and vision extraction (an LLM reads the rendered page). Round 2 added scale calibration from a known dimension, label–to–region association, geometry cleanup, a vision grid overlay, and a vision↔vector cross-check so the two methods can confirm each other. Needs the [pdf] extra.

6.3 DXF export

dxf_export writes a cross-section back out to DXF — surface, soil boundaries, water table, nails/anchors, and annotations — so a model built or checked in the toolkit can return to CAD.

6.4 Staged, human-gated model setup (geo_project)

geo_project is a canonical project document for building 2D LE/FEM models in stages with confirmation gates. The agent never trusts its own read of a drawing: it ingests geometry with provenance quarantine, then renders an echo-back cross-section so a human visually confirms the numbers before they enter the model. It is wired to the v2 deep agent as an opt-in model-setup sub-agent.

6.5 Calc-package reporting

calc_package turns a module result into a Mathcad-style calculation package — HTML or LaTeX, with figures and equation traces — for about a dozen of the analysis modules. On a system with pdflatex it can emit PDF; on Databricks (no LaTeX), emit the self-contained HTML and print it to PDF from the browser. It needs the [calc] extra (Jinja2), plus [plot] for figures and [interactive] for the Plotly viewers.

Chapter 7Reliability & probabilistic analysis

This is the payoff of the whole architecture. Soil properties carry coefficients of variation of 10–40% — far larger than structural materials — so the honest deliverable is not a lone factor of safety but a reliability index β and a probability of failure Pf. The reliability module turns any deterministic method into a probabilistic one.

7.1 Declare the uncertainty, pick an engine

Declare the uncertain inputs as random variables, hand the engine a performance function g(values) that returns a factor of safety or a margin, and pick an engine. All four share the same g() contract:

EngineCostWhat it does
FOSMcheapFirst-Order Second-Moment — propagates means and variances for an instant β, no sampling
PEMrobustRosenblueth point-estimate — evaluates g() at ± points; handles non-linearity without a derivative
Monte Carloexact-ishSamples the joint distribution N times and counts failures; correlations via Cholesky, optional Latin Hypercube
FORMefficientNative first-order reliability — finds the design point; β at a fraction of Monte Carlo’s calls
Worked example

Ask → Resistance R (mean 500, COV 20%, lognormal) against load S (mean 300, COV 15%) — 50,000 Monte-Carlo trials: what is the reliability index and the probability of failure?

call_agent(
    agent_name='reliability',
    method='monte_carlo',
    parameters={
        "variables": {
                "R": {
                        "mean": 500.0,
                        "cov": 0.2,
                        "dist": "lognormal"
                },
                "S": {
                        "mean": 300.0,
                        "cov": 0.15,
                        "dist": "normal"
                }
        },
        "g_expression": "R - S",
        "convention": "margin",
        "n": 50000,
        "seed": 42
    },
)
Representative output (real, from the shipped code)
engine: monte_carlo
convention: margin
n: 50000
n_failed: 1008
pf: 0.0202
pf_ci95: [2 entries]
g_mean: 199.4937
g_std: 109.7902
g_cov: 0.5503
g_min: -175.3176
g_max: 803.6505
g_median: 191.5376
percentiles: {p1=-20.952, p5=34.8924, p10=66.1934, p50=191.5376, p90=343.9452, p95=394.0009}
beta_normal: 1.817
… (additional fields in the full result dict)

This is the payoff of the whole architecture: any deterministic method plugs into the same g() contract and returns β and Pf instead of a lone number.

7.2 Don’t assume a COV — look it up

cov_guidance is a queryable knowledge base of published coefficients of variation (Duncan 2000, TC304, Phoon & Kulhawy) keyed by soil property, so the input uncertainty is defensible rather than assumed. variance_reduction applies Vanmarcke spatial averaging — a footing averages over its footprint, a long slope samples many weak and strong zones, so the variance that actually matters is reduced over the volume the structure loads. combined_cov composes several sources of uncertainty.

7.3 Which input governs? — global sensitivity

salib wraps SALib for variance-based global sensitivity: Sobol indices and Morris screening answer which input drives the spread of the answer, so the site investigation and the design effort go where they matter. pystra adds a dedicated structural reliability engine (FORM / SORM / Monte Carlo) for limit-state functions.

7.4 Probabilistic paths that ship out of the box

The reliability wrappers — bearing_capacity_reliability, axial_pile_reliability, and slope_reliability — and the slope-stability module’s built-in FOSM and Monte-Carlo FOS mean the probabilistic path is available directly, without hand-wiring the performance function for the most common problems.

Chapter 8Validation basis

42
published problems checked
75
individual module-vs-source comparisons
53
PASS (within stated tolerance)
0
unexplained discrepancies

Beyond the per-module unit suites (which regress each method against textbook answers), the package carries a published-example validation layer: real worked examples from the design manuals and FE verification suites, with complete numeric inputs and published numeric answers, run through the analysis modules offline. The problems (V-001…V-040) and their sources are in validation_examples/INVENTORY.md; the run-by-run verdicts are in validation_examples/RESULTS.md. Flagship modules additionally carry a VALIDATION.md (slope_stability vs Fredlund & Krahn 1977 / ACADS / Duncan; fem2d vs Griffiths & Lane and the Prandtl solution; lateral_pile vs a COM624P oracle). Verdicts are graded honestly: PASS (reproduces the published answer within tolerance), CONVENTION (a defensibly different but documented convention — the module is not tuned to the one example), and N/A (scope) (the module implements a different method than the example — a documented coverage gap, not a failure). Across 75 comparisons there were zero unexplained discrepancies.

V-037slope_stabilityRapid drawdown — USACE 2-stageEM 1110-2-1902 / Slide2 #95PASS
V-039slope_stabilityNewmark seismic sliding block + Jibson (2007)Slide2 #104 / Tutorial 28PASS
V-040slope_stabilityStabilizing micro-piles (Ito & Matsui 1975)Yamagami 2000 / Slide2 #54CONVENTION

The table above is a representative selection; the complete run-by-run record — every delta, tolerance, and the reasoning behind each convention/scope verdict — is in validation_examples/RESULTS.md.

8.2 How to read the verdicts

PASS

The module reproduces the published answer within the stated tolerance. Example: the Mononobe–Okabe seismic coefficient KAE reproduces the GEC-11 value to within 0.06%; the Fellenius/Bishop factors of safety match the Caltrans slice table to the printed digit.

CONVENTION

The module and the example use a defensibly different convention, and the delta is documented — the module is not tuned to the one example. Example: for the GEC-6 spread footing, the packaged high-level call applies Vesic depth factors while the example deliberately sets them to 1.0 for cohesive overburden; assembled the example’s way, the module recovers the published closed form exactly.

N/A (scope)

The module implements a different method than the example — a documented coverage gap, not a failure. Example: a slope problem whose pore pressure is supplied as an interpolated flow-net grid, which the module (piezometric surface or per-layer ru) does not accept.

The philosophy is visible in these notes: where the module and a source differ, the manual says why, in the source’s own terms, rather than quietly fitting the code to one benchmark. Several checks even surfaced errors in the published examples (for instance an under-iterated Bishop value that the module iterates to convergence).

Chapter 9Limitations & responsible use

Everything in the disclaimer at the front of this manual applies. This chapter makes the boundaries concrete, because knowing where a tool stops is part of using it well.

9.1 It is a multiplier for judgment, not a replacement

The toolkit runs the methods; it does not know your site and cannot exercise engineering judgment. A qualified, licensed professional engineer familiar with the site must independently review every input, assumption, method selection, and result before it is relied upon. Using this software creates no engineer-of-record relationship.

9.2 Validation covers only the documented cases

Agreement on a benchmark (Chapter 8) does not certify correctness for any other geometry, parameter range, or loading condition. The absence of a validation entry means a result has not been independently checked here. Read the module’s DESIGN.md and VALIDATION.md for its exact scope, sign conventions, and edge cases before trusting it on a new problem.

9.3 Known method boundaries

A few honest scope notes drawn straight from the validation record:

  • Diesel-hammer drivability in wave_equation is an energy–velocity approximation, not a GRLWEAP combustion + ram-cycle model; treat diesel bearing graphs as a trend, not a tie-out.
  • slope_stability accepts a piezometric surface or per-layer ru, not an arbitrary interpolated pore-pressure grid; its tension crack is entry-side and keeps the cracked wedge as driving soil (a conservative convention).
  • ground_improvement uses an equal-strain settlement-reduction model for aggregate piers, not the GEC-13 stiffness-modulus two-layer method; the Priebe curve is GEC-13's printed curve (φ = 37.5°) and depends on the area-ratio convention you feed it.
  • The high-level bearing_capacity call applies Vesic depth factors and an effective-unit-weight groundwater model — defensible, but different from an AASHTO Cw groundwater correction; know which convention your check needs.
  • Soldier-pile arching and the FHWA apparent-diagram single-anchor embedment solver are documented gaps in soe/sheet_pile.

9.4 Treat agent output with particular care

The LLM agent can select the wrong method, mis-transcribe a value, or read a chart imperfectly. Its answers are a starting point for review, never a final basis for design. Inspect the tool calls (result.tool_calls, or verbose=True) — the methods and parameters actually used — not just the prose. Confirm the inputs and units: everything is SI, and mis-scaled units are the user’s responsibility to catch.

The bottom line

Responsibility for the safety, adequacy, and code-compliance of any design remains entirely with the licensed professional engineer who adopts it. This software is provided under the MIT License “AS IS”, without warranty of any kind.
